item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Three Important Questions for Dodgers Before 2027
item.dc:creator: Katherine Wacker

item.content:encoded:
Last season ended in disappointment for the Los Angeles Dodgers. Now, they must assess themselves as they prepare for the future. Here are three questions they must ask if they want to continue their prolonged success into 2027 and beyond.
In the Market for Pitching Again?
Los Angeles knows better than most that one can never have enough pitching. To that end, they traded for Tarik Skubal at the trade deadline this year. Now, are they willing to keep him? The left-hander is expected to earn a pretty penny this year. Moreover, he has Scott Boras as his agent and an abbreviated window with which to negotiate as December 1 approaches. Los Angeles and President of Baseball Operations Andrew Friedman have plenty of money at their disposal, provided that their owner doesn't sell the team.
However, Los Angeles, with a few notable exceptions, is very hesitant to dole out long-term contracts to a player entering free agency who is entering his third decade. The more likely option for a mutual agreement would be a shorter deal in length with a higher AAV, similar to the Kyle Tucker deal. It is said that Los Angeles has some competition for the left-hander's services; the New York Mets and Chicago Cubs are also interested. Skubal did seem to like it in Los Angeles, but it's still a question where he will end up. However, those in the know expect a deal signed by December 1.
The Youth Movement?
Los Angeles has the oldest roster in baseball, and it showed during the National League Championship Series against the World Champion Milwaukee Brewers. The question is how young will the Dodgers go without compromising the veteran core? There is no question that there will be some turnover on the margins. Enrique and Teoscar Hernandez will probably be on different teams in 2027. Josue DePaula will probably cement his place on the roster. Do they sign or trade for a shortstop like Elly de La Cruz? Will they move Mookie Betts to second base to preserve him from wear and tear on his body?
Friedman, in his year-end press conference, addressed the age of the players, but he didn't seem overly concerned right now. He pointed out that whoever they place on the roster must be major-league ready and fit the team's needs. It will be interesting to see the evolution of the roster as the offseason progresses.
Andrew Friedman and Brandon Gomes address Ohtani’s health and 2027 pitching plans, Skubal’s free agency, De Paula and Sasaki’s futures, Miguel Rojas’ next role, the aging roster and claims the Dodgers’ dynasty is over. Watch the full press conference:
https://t.co/ghginLTHqM
— DodgersBeat | Dodgers News & Interviews (@DodgersBeat) October 21, 2026
Utilization of Ohtani
Probably, the most impactful question the Dodgers need to answer going forward is how to keep Shohei Ohtani healthy. Los Angeles gave lip service to limitations on the two-way player's workload last year. However, there was a two-month period when he didn't get a day off. Ohtani says he wants to pitch in 2027, and the Dodgers "are excited" at the prospect. If that is true, both parties need to get together to come up with an effective approach. This plan probably should include more days completely out of the lineup.
Admittedly, Ohtani is clearly "one of one," and the road ahead is unprecedented. However, the Dodgers need to figure something out. A wounded superstar hampered the Dodgers' chances in the postseason this past season. If the Dodgers want to keep making deep runs in October, Ohtani must be as healthy as he can be, even at the expense of his pitching.
The Last Word
Of course, all the answers to these questions largely depend on whether there is a season in 2027. With the lockout looming, Los Angeles will have to figure out where and when to sign free agents and how to deploy Ohtani in what could be a truncated season. The Commissioner has proposed a stay on the implementation of a salary cap. It remains to be seen if the players take him up on the offer. If nothing changes, it could be a long winter with plenty of time for the Dodgers to ponder questions.

item.content:encoded:
In the immortal words of former Indianapolis Colts football coach Jim Mora:
Playoffs? Playoffs? Playoffs!
Yeah, playoffs.
The postseason has arrived. And it will be a busy one for Lancaster-Lebanon League pigskin teams, with 19 squads spread out over five District 3 brackets.
There are 11 games on tap for Friday — multiple teams in the league. received first-round byes and will be idle in Week 11 — with nine District 3 matchups and a pair of Eastern Conference games featuring 15 L-L League teams on the slate.
Win and advance. Lose and report directly to winter sports practice. We have reached that stage of the season.
Here’s a Week 11 preview — including key players to watch and predictions — as the postseason gets cranked up. All games are Friday at 7 p.m. unless noted.
Playoffs, Mr. Mora. Playoffs indeed.
Predictions: 16-3 last week; 167-46 overall.
District 3 Class 6A first round
No. 10 Hempfield (5-5) at No. 7 Cedar Crest (7-3)
Rematch alert: The Falcons clipped the Black Knights 28-19 in a Section 1 clash back in Week 4, and Cedar Crest KO’d Hempfield 49-29 in a district 6A first-round game in 2024. Plenty of familiarity in this scrap. This is the 17th district trip for the Knights, who are 9-16; the Falcons are here for the fourth straight year and the 10th time overall, and they’re 3-9. Winner is at No. 2 Manheim Township (9-1) in the quarterfinals. That will be another rematch, no matter the Blue Streaks’ opponent.
Key kid: Hempfield RB Ramel Lyles leads all Section 1 backs with 923 rushing yards and 14 TD runs. Four times this season he has rushed for 150 or more yards in a game, including 168 yards and two TDs last week against Manheim Township.
The pick: Knights take flight, knock off Falcons.
No. 9 Cumberland Valley (5-5) at No. 8 Penn Manor (6-4)
This is old hat for the Mid-Penn Commonwealth Eagles, who are making their 34th district trip, and they’re 52-20 with 13 titles in 21 championship games. They are District 3 royalty, regardless of their record or seed. The upstart Comets are back in districts for the first time since 2014 — which capped a run of eight straight trips — and they’re 5-8. Winner is at No. 1 Central York (8-2) in the quarterfinals.
Key kids: CV LB Jayden Holmes has 61 tackles, nine sticks for losses, three sacks and two fumble recoveries. He’ll have his eyes peeled on shifty PM backs Jalen Dupree and Randy Guthrie, who have combined for 866 rushing yards, 62 receptions for 638 yards, and 22 TDs between them.
The pick: Tradition rarely sleeps; Eagles edge Comets.
District 3 Class 5A first round
No. 11 Northeastern York (8-2) at No. 6 Conestoga Valley (8-2)
The Bobcats, out of SCAC Division II, are in districts for the seventh time — and for the first time since 2019 — and they’re 1-6. That win was against Northern Lebanon in 2014. The Buckskins are here for the fourth year in a row and for the 15th time overall, and they’re 10-13 with one crown. CV has been bounced by Section 2 foe Exeter the last two seasons. Winner is at No. 3 Solanco (9-1) in the quarterfinals.
Key kids: NY LB Antonio Lee has 67 tackles, with nine hits for losses and 1.5 sacks. Might he spy CV dual-threat QB Camryn Bair? He’s thrown for 1,332 yards, needs 124 yards for 1,000 rushing yards, and he has accounted for 29 touchdowns.
The pick: Bucks bushwhack Bobcats.
No. 9 Cocalico (6-4) at No. 8 Dover (8-2)
Cocalico is in districts for the 26th time, and is 34-20 with five championships, including back-to-back 5A crowns in 2022-23. Dover, out of SCAC Division II, is here for the 10th time — and is 2-9 — and for the first time since 2023, when it fell to Conestoga Valley in a 5A first-rounder. Winner is at No. 1 Twin Valley (10-0) in the quarterfinals. Dover’s top priority: Curtailing Cocalico’s rushing attack, which has amassed 2,945 rushing yards, third-most in the L-L League.
Key kids: Dover QB Iyon Valenti is 96-for-198 for 1,765 yards with 23 TD tosses, and he has four receivers with 350 or more receiving yards — including Eli Smyser, who averages 30.9 yards a catch, and Lincoln Decker and Mimi Valenti, who each have seven TD grabs — at his disposal.
The pick: In a battle of Eagles, Cocalico clips Dover.
No. 10 Lower Dauphin (6-4) at No. 7 Ephrata (8-2)
The Falcons, who call the Mid-Penn Keystone home, are here for the fourth straight year and the 18th time overall, and they’re 11-14 with three championships. The Mountaineers, who are here for the third time, edged LD 14-13 in a 5A opener in 2023, when Ephrata reached the title game. Prior to that, the Mounts weren’t in districts since 1987. Winner is at No. 2 Northern York (9-1) in the quarterfinals.
Key kids: LD RB Connor Kreiser has rushed for 1,172 yards with 20 TD runs. Ephrata LB Caleb Rice (107 tackles, 7.5 TFL, 7 QB hurries) will have Kreiser in his crosshairs.
The pick: Mounts outlast Falcons.
No. 12 Hershey (6-4) at No. 5 Exeter (8-2)
The Trojans, out of the Mid-Penn Keystone, are here for the 15th time, and they’re 8-13 with one title. Hershey eliminated Exeter 28-27 in a 5A opener in 2021. The Eagles are here for the 17th time, and they’re 15-15 with one crown. Exeter is making its sixth straight trip, and is 11-4 in district games over the last five years. Winner is at No. 4 Spring Grove (8-2) in the quarterfinals.
Key kids: Hershey LB Caine Stepp has 58 tackles, with 10 sticks for losses, two sacks and a trio of fumble recoveries. He’ll try and contain Exeter backs Josh Jackson (874 yards, 6 TDs) and Donovyn Alvarez (578 yards, 8 TDs).
The pick: Eagles trip up Trojans.
District 3 Class 4A first round
No. 9 Elco (6-4) at No. 8 Conrad Weiser (6-4)
These backyard rivals squared off in a Section 4 game back in Week 4, and the Raiders stopped the Scouts 21-12 behind Gavin Yeiser, who rushed for 117 yards and two TDs. The win-or-go-home rematch will also be in Robesonia. Elco is here for the 11th time and is 5-10. The Raiders are making their fourth straight trip, and they’ve won three first-round games in a row. Weiser is here for the 19th time and is 13-18; the Scouts are 0-4 in their last four trips. Winner is at No. 1 West York (10-0) in the quarterfinals; the Bulldogs are the top-ranked 4A team in the state.
Key kid: CW RB-DB Kole Kupper has rushed for 1,389 yards with 22 TD runs, he has 13 catches, including a TD grab, 490 punt- and kick-return yards, plus 14 tackles and an interception.
The pick: Scouts get revenge, slither past Raiders.
No. 10 Northern Lebanon (6-4) at No. 7 Susquehannock (6-4)
The Vikings are back in districts for the first time since 2019, and for the eighth time overall. NL is 0-7 in district games, and is looking to snap that skid. The Warriors, out of SCAC Division II, are here for the fifth time, and they’re 1-4. That win came back in 2006, and this is the first time Susky will play an L-L League entrant in districts. Winner is at No. 2 Hanover (10-0) in the quarterfinals.
Key kids: Susky DE Dylan LaGore has been a backfield-crasher with 37 tackles, 13 stops for losses, 12 sacks and 11 QB hurries. He’ll try to deny NL RB Brady Ryan, who has rushed for 1,241 yards and 16 TDs.
The pick: Warriors withstand Vikings.
District 3 Class 2A semifinals
No. 3 Columbia (4-6) at No. 2 Upper Dauphin (6-4)
The Crimson Tide are here for the 21st time and are 6-18 with a pair of championships. The Trojans, out of the Mid-Penn Capital, are here for the 12th time, and they’re 4-10, including a 2A title in 2019. UD outlasted Columbia 58-48 in a 2A semifinal in 2021. Winner gets No. 1 York Catholic (6-4) or No. 4 Newport (5-5) in the championship.
Key kid: UD RB Chris McClain has scooted for 1,150 yards with 15 TD runs, including a 108-yard, three-TD night last week against Steel-High. Columbia must keep him contained.
The pick: Trojans tackle Tide.
Eastern Conference Class 4A
Daniel Boone (2-8) at Fleetwood (4-6)
The Blazers snapped a string of three straight 1-9 seasons, and garnered enough power points to squeeze into this EC matchup. The Tigers’ last EC appearance was a memorable one; Fleetwood trailed 34-7 before rallying past Shamokin 42-41 in the 2023 4A game. Boone is in an EC game for the first time since 2005, and is 1-2; the Tigers are 3-2 in EC games, including the win in 2023, and a victory over Boyertown in 2021. Boone leads this series 7-2 — Fleetwood won the last meeting 42-0 in 2023 — and the Blazers and the Tigers will square off for the first time in a postseason game.
Key kid: In three games since taking over the starting QB duties, Boone’s John Burmester is 39-for-85 for 523 yards with four TD tosses.
The pick: Tigers tame Blazers.
Eastern Conference Class 3A
Hamburg (6-4) at Berks Catholic (6-4), 6 p.m.
It will be a Section 5 rematch when the Hawks and Saints collide; BC beat Hamburg 38-7 back in Week 4 to grab a 13-0 lead in the series. This is BC’s third EC appearance, and the Saints are 2-0, with a 49-14 win over Pine Grove in 2022 and a 40-21 victory over Hamburg in 2023. The Hawks are here for the seventh time; they’re 1-5, and that was a 28-0 win over Big Spring in 2019. The Saints’ top priority will be slowing down Hawks’ RB Blaise Ernst, who motored for 270 yards and three TDs in a Week 10 win over Kutztown. BC was the last team out in the district 3A race; the Saints are riding a five-game winning streak, but were leapfrogged by Trinity at the wire.
Key kid: BC RB Coy Koller has rushed for 927 yards — 73 shy of 1,000 — with 10 TD runs, including a 149-yard, four-TD effort in a Week 10 win over Lancaster Catholic.
The pick: Saints handle Hawks.

item.content:encoded:
The coaching changes continue for the Red Sox.
The Boston Red Sox coaching staff is continuing to take shape. A week after hiring Houston Astros fielding coordinator Jason Bell as outfield instructor, Chris Cotillo and Sean McAdam of MassLive.com report that the Red Sox are hiring New York Yankees Triple-A manager Shelley Duncan to join manager Chad Tracy’s staff.
About Duncan
A seven-year veteran, Duncan played outfield and designated hitter for the Yankees, Cleveland, and the Tampa Bay Rays. After his playing days ended in 2014, Duncan moved into coaching, becoming the Low-A manager for the Arizona Diamondbacks affiliate. After spending two seasons in Low-A and another one in High-A, Duncan was promoted to Double-A manager, where he won the 2018 Southern League Championship with the Jackson Generals.
After the 2018 season, the Toronto Blue Jays hired Duncan as major league field coordinator. After two seasons in Toronto, the Chicago White Sox hired Duncan as analytics coordinator. Duncan returned to the minor leagues in 2023, joining the team that drafted him, the Yankees, as Triple-A manager.
Under Duncan’s leadership, Scranton-Wilkes-Barre went 327-263. The former outfielder was named the 2025 International League Manager of the Year.
Like Bell, Duncan’s role on the staff is unclear. The team has openings at both first- and third-base coach positions after reassigning interim coaches Chad Epperson and Pablo Cabrera to different positions in the organization.
In other Red Sox news
After designating reliever Eduardo Rivera for assignment on Monday, the 23-year-old left-hander was traded to the St. Louis Cardinals on Tuesday in exchange for 18-year-old pitching prospect Juan Carlos Garcia. Rivera spent most of the season in Triple-A, posting a 2.96 ERA in 24 appearances and striking out 27.7 percent of the batters he faced. While Garcia made 11 starts in the Dominican Summer League, posting a 4.40 ERA, striking out 39 and walking 10.
Red Sox infield prospect Antonio Anderson has been a standout in the Arizona Fall League. In 16 games for the Mesa Solar Sox, the 21-year-old is hitting .361/.500/.623/1.123 with three home runs and five doubles, driving in 20 runs, leading Mesa in all seven categories. Anderson earned a spot on the American League Fall-Star team for his performance. The Arizona League Fall-Star Game is set for Sunday at 8:00 p.m. ET and will air on MLB Network. In addition to being named a Fall-Star, Anderson will participate in the AFL Home Run Derby, which will be held Saturday night at 8:00 p.m. ET and, like the All-Star Game, will air on MLB Network.

item.content:encoded:
Avanza caso Guardians: Señalan a Emmanuel Clase y Luis Ortiz por vender información de sus lanzamientos
Los abogados defensores argumentan que los peloteros dominicanos fueron víctimas de engaños por parte de un apostador profesional.
Los lanzadores de los Cleveland Guardians, Emmanuel Clase y Luis Ortiz, fueron señalados como “tramposos” por la fiscalía este miércoles durante los alegatos de apertura en un juicio penal por fraude en Nueva York, caso que ha puesto bajo la lupa la amenaza que representan los apostadores en el béisbol de las Grandes Ligas.
La fiscal federal adjunta, Rebecca Urquiola, dijo a un jurado en Brooklyn que Clase entabló amistad con un apostador deportivo en la República Dominicana a principios de 2023, compartiendo afición por los dominós y las peleas de gallos.
Según la parte acusadora, Clase aceptó informarle sobre el tipo de lanzamientos que realizaría en determinados encuentros, lo que permitió a los apostadores obtener ganancias de al menos 460,000 dólares en plataformas de apuestas en vivo.
“Los acusados, Emmanuel Clase y Luis Ortiz, son unos tramposos. Vendieron sus lanzamientos”, declaró Urquiola ante los jurados.
Las acusaciones de la fiscalía y los detalles de la red
El excerrador estrella de los Guardians y el abridor Ortiz se han declarado no culpables de los cargos de conspiración y se encuentran con licencia sin goce de sueldo desde que fueron arrestados en noviembre de 2025.
La fiscalía sostiene que Clase comenzó a proveer información sobre sus lanzamientos a los apostadores en 2023 y posteriormente reclutó a Ortiz dentro del esquema durante la temporada 2025.
Urquiola detalló que existen mensajes de texto donde los serpentineros describían los pitcheos arreglados utilizando palabras clave como "pollo" o "gallo", evidencia que sumada a los testimonios comprobará la responsabilidad de los peloteros.
Afirman que fueron víctimas de engaño
Por su parte, los abogados defensores argumentaron que sus clientes son inocentes y que el apostador involucrado, identificado como Enoc Peña, se aprovechó de la cercanía con Clase para inventar información y vendérsela a otros apostadores.
Michael Bronson, abogado de Clase, señaló que el relevista era una superestrella de 25 años en 2023 cuando conoció a Peña, un apostador de 41 años con un historial de engaños que vio en el jugador una oportunidad de negocio.
Afirmó además que el apostador perdió más de 200 apuestas intentando adivinar los lanzamientos.
En tanto, Samuel Landes, representante legal de Luis Ortiz, indicó al jurado que el lanzador no tuvo contacto con los apostadores y que el caso en su contra se reduce únicamente a dos lanzamientos marcados como bolas.
“Eso no es una conspiración. Eso es simplemente béisbol”, expresó Landes tras cuestionar por qué Ortiz arriesgaría una carrera millonaria por un pago de 5,000 dólares.
El proceso judicial continuará en los próximos días en la corte de Brooklyn, donde se determinará la situación legal de ambos peloteros caribeños.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox last played on September 30.
They lost to the New York Yankees in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series.
That said, the Red Sox still did a good job of getting into the 2026 MLB playoffs under manager Chad Tracy.
9-Year MLB Veteran Becomes Boston Red Sox Free Agent
This week, a player within the Red Sox’ organization became a free agent.
John Brebbia will be available to sign with any team in the MLB.
MLB.com wrote (on November 2): “RHP John Brebbia elected free agency.”
John Brebbia #63 of the Colorado Rockies delivers a pitch against the San Diego Padres during the fourth inning of a spring training game at Salt River Fields at Talking Stick on February 27, 2026 in Scottsdale, Arizona.
Brebbia did not appear in a game for the Red Sox at the MLB level.
He had signed with the organization during the middle of the season.
MLB.com wrote (on August 7): “Boston Red Sox signed free agent RHP John Brebbia to a minor league contract.”
Looking At Brebbia
Pitcher John Brebbia #60 of the St. Louis Cardinals throws in the bottom of 9th inning during the game three of Japan and MLB All Stars at Tokyo Dome on November 11, 2018 in Tokyo, Japan.
Brebbia was picked in the 30th round of the 2011 MLB Draft.
He spent the first three seasons of his MLB career with the St. Louis Cardinals.
Following St. Louis, Brebbia signed with the San Francisco Giants.
MLB.com wrote (on December 21, 2020): “San Francisco Giants signed free agent RHP John Brebbia.”
John Brebbia #59 of the San Francisco Giants pitches in the top of the first inning against the Chicago Cubs at Oracle Park on June 11, 2023 in San Francisco, California.
Brebbia later had stops with the Chicago White Sox, Atlanta Braves, Detroit Tigers and Colorado Rockies.
He most recently pitched for the Rockies in 2026.
The 36-year-old went 0-0 with a 10.38 ERA in three games.
Looking At The Red Sox Right Now
Boston Red Sox Interim Manager Chad Tracy looks on from the dugout during the first inning at Fenway Park on May 01, 2026 in Boston, Massachusetts.
The Red Sox last won a World Series title in 2018.
They finished this past year as the third-place team in the American League East with an 87-75 record in 162 games.

item.content:encoded:
Los Boston Red Sox, tras otra eliminación temprana en los playoffs, esta vez en la ronda de comodines, buscan reforzarse para llegar más lejos en 2027. Pero cuánto se moverá Craig Breslow, director de operaciones de béisbol, en el mercado de cambios sigue siendo la gran incógnita que ocupará a los aficionados de los Red Sox durante los próximos meses.
Pero los conductores de “Play Tessie” se adelantaron a Breslow el miércoles: en la última edición de su popular pódcast afiliado a WEEI, plantearon un cambio para los Red Sox que aliviaría la saturación de jardineros del equipo y les daría un lanzador derecho elegido en la segunda ronda del draft y a un jugador que ha logrado tres temporadas con al menos 20 jonrones y 20 bases robadas.
¿Cuál es la propuesta? Según explicó Nat “Gordo” Gordon, conductor de “Play Tessie”, Boston recibiría a Oneil Cruz y Mitch Keller de los Pittsburgh Pirates a cambio de Jarren Duran y otros tres integrantes del equipo de Grandes Ligas. La propuesta no contempla un intercambio de prospectos.
Cruz aportaría una combinación poco común de velocidad y poder a una alineación que necesita ambas cosas, pero el precio incluye al abridor zurdo Jake Bennett además de Jarren Duran, y los conductores no coinciden en si alguno de los equipos aceptaría.
Gordon armó el acuerdo para el primer segmento de “¿Quién dice que no?” del programa en esta temporada baja. Boston enviaría a Bennett, Duran, Mickey Gasper y el contrato de Masataka Yoshida, al que le queda un año por 18 millones de dólares, a los Pirates. Su propuesta se apoya en la temporada 2026 de Cruz.
“Conectó 20 jonrones y robó 30 bases en 97 partidos”, dijo Gordon el miércoles en el pódcast Play Tessie de WEEI.
Cruz, bateador zurdo de 6 pies y 7 pulgadas nacido el 4 de octubre de 1998 en Nizao, República Dominicana, tiene una línea ofensiva de .243/.322/.438 con 80 jonrones en su carrera y 103 bases robadas en 476 partidos desde su debut en 2021. En 2026 bateó .280/.368/.486 en 97 partidos, acumuló 2.8 de WAR y se perdió partidos por fracturas sin desplazamiento en los metacarpianos de la mano izquierda.
Keller, lanzador derecho de 6 pies y 3 pulgadas nacido el 4 de abril de 1996 en Cedar Rapids, Iowa, fue elegido por los Pirates en la segunda ronda del draft de 2014. Este año, pese a problemas en el hombro, terminó con marca de 6-8 y efectividad de 5.29, además de un WHIP de 1.37 en 115 2/3 entradas durante 22 aperturas. Su marca de por vida es de 48-73 con efectividad de 4.60. En 2024, firmó una extensión de cinco años por 77 millones de dólares, de la que restan unos 18 millones para 2027 y 20 millones para 2028.
Bennett, zurdo de 6 pies y 6 pulgadas nacido el 2 de diciembre de 2000 en Tulsa, Oklahoma, llegó de Washington a cambio de Luis Perales en diciembre de 2025 y debutó el 1 de mayo. Terminó con marca de 9-7 y efectividad de 3.65, y ponchó a 91 bateadores en 113 1/3 entradas durante 19 aperturas.
Duran, veloz jardinero de 6 pies nacido el 5 de septiembre de 1996 en Corona, California, y elegido por los Red Sox en el draft de 2018, fue seleccionado para el Juego de Estrellas de 2024 y ganó el premio al Jugador Más Valioso de ese partido. Esa temporada bateó .285/.342/.492 con 21 jonrones y 34 bases robadas. En 2026 bajó a .207/.266/.361, con 20 jonrones y 21 bases robadas en 151 partidos, y se proyecta que gane unos 11 millones de dólares mediante arbitraje salarial.
Gasper, bateador ambidiestro de 5 pies y 9 pulgadas nacido el 11 de octubre de 1995 en New Hampshire y elegido por los Yankees en el draft de 2018, bateó .251/.357/.466 con 10 jonrones en 67 partidos.
Yoshida, nacido el 15 de julio de 1993 en Japón, firmó un contrato de cinco años por 90 millones de dólares que vence después de 2027. Este año bateó .274/.347/.399 en 87 partidos.
El lugar de Oneil Cruz en la alineación de los Boston Red Sox
Cruz enfrentó rectas en el 49.5% de los lanzamientos durante la mejor temporada ofensiva de su carrera, según Gordon.
“Oneil Cruz sabe batear lanzamientos a esa velocidad”, dijo el conductor del pódcast. Gordon señaló que los lanzamientos de alta velocidad son un punto débil de Boston, pero advirtió que la muestra abarca aproximadamente una temporada.
El copresentador Pat Brown señaló la otra cara de la moneda.
“Estuvo en el primer percentil en tasa de ponches y en el segundo percentil en tasa de swings fallidos. Eso añade mucho riesgo”, dijo Brown. Cruz registró un OPS de .676 en 2025, mientras que su .854 de 2026 supera con creces el .760 de su carrera.
La posición es una duda mayor. Gordon descartó el campo corto y dejó abiertas las demás opciones. “Probablemente jugaría sobre todo como jardinero y bateador designado, pero lo traerías por su bate y por lo que puede aportar a la ofensiva”, dijo Gordon.
Boston ya cuenta en los jardines con Roman Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela y Wilyer Abreu, mientras que Rafaela, Abreu y el tercera base Caleb Durbin ganaron Guantes de Oro Rawlings en 2026. Las métricas defensivas de Cruz en el jardín central han sido dispares o desfavorables. “Fue terrible en el campo corto”, dijo Pat. Sammy consideró que la tercera base sería la mejor opción, pero Durbin ocupa ese puesto. El lugar disponible es el de bateador designado, y Yoshida y Gasper, quienes lo ocupan ahora, saldrían del equipo según la propuesta de “Play Tessie”.
La rotación también saldría perjudicada.
“Si Keller forma parte del cambio, ocuparía el lugar de Jake Bennett”, dijo Gordon.
“Tu rotación probablemente bajaría un poco de nivel”, añadió el copresentador Sammy James. Keller tampoco reemplaza a Sonny Gray. Gray se convirtió en agente libre en octubre tras terminar con marca de 18-5, efectividad de 2.72 y 169 entradas lanzadas, frente a la efectividad de 5.29 de Keller.
¿Aceptarían los Boston Red Sox y los Pirates el cambio por Oneil Cruz?
Los Pirates se desprenderían de unos 38 millones de dólares del contrato de Keller y asumirían los 18 millones de Yoshida: un ahorro aproximado de 20 millones, según los cálculos de Gordon y James. Los 11 millones que Duran cobraría mediante arbitraje salarial y los 7 millones proyectados para Cruz reducen esa diferencia.
“Para un equipo de Grandes Ligas, no es tanto. Pero los Pirates solo son un equipo de Grandes Ligas en términos técnicos”, bromeó James.
Brown cree que Pittsburgh aceptaría el cambio.
“Tienen tan poco dinero que aceptarían perder lo que Oneil Cruz podría aportarles con tal de liberar algo de presupuesto”, dijo. Brown cree que Boston rechazaría el acuerdo.
“Cambias a Yoshida, pero básicamente añades otro año de Yoshida”, dijo Brown.
James opinó que ambos equipos dirían que no, aunque Pittsburgh estaría cerca de aceptar.
“Los Pirates están muy cerca de aceptarlo”, dijo Sammy. Gordon estuvo de acuerdo y señaló las prioridades de Boston.
“Si les presentas esto directamente a las directivas, ambas dirían: ‘Gracias, pero no’”, dijo Gordo. Añadió que los Red Sox necesitan “más certezas sobre el bate que incorporaríamos”.
El resultado financiero favorece a Pittsburgh. Los Pirates se liberan del salario de Keller en 2028, mientras que Boston prolonga sus compromisos hasta esa temporada y entrega a Bennett, con su efectividad de 3.65 y los años que aún podría mantenerlo bajo control contractual. Los conductores señalaron que Boston conservaría a prospectos como Franklin Arias y Payton Tolle, pero solo sumaría un bateador de rendimiento muy incierto. La ofensiva mejoraría únicamente si Cruz repite lo que hizo en 2026. La defensa ganaría poco.

item.title: [Heavy.com] Red Sox Trade Pitch Lands Oneil Cruz in 6-Player Jarren Duran-Led Blockbuster
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Vankin
item.description: The Boston Red Sox, after another early exit from the playoffs at the Wild Card stage, are looking to retool for a deeper run in 2027. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox, after another early exit from the playoffs at the Wild Card stage, are looking to retool for a deeper run in 2027. But how active chief baseball officer Craig Breslow will be on the trade market hangs as an unresolved question for Red Sox Nation to obsess over for the next several months.
But the hosts of “Play Tessie” got a jump on Breslow Wednesday when, in the latest edition of their popular WEEI-affiliated podcast, they presented the Red Sox with a trade pitch that would help ease the team’s outfield logjam while bringing in a former second-round pick righthander and a three-time member of the 20-20 club.
What’s the trade pitch? As outlined by “Play Tessie” host Nat “Gordo” Gordon, Boston would land Oneil Cruz and Mitch Keller from the Pittsburgh Pirates for Jarren Duran and three other current members of the major league club. A prospect swap doesn’t figure into their proposed deal.
Cruz brings rare speed and power to a lineup that needs both, but the price includes left-handed starter Jake Bennett as well as Jarren Duran, and the hosts split on whether either club says yes.
Gordon built the deal for the show’s first “Who Says No” segment of the offseason. Boston would send Bennett, Duran, Mickey Gasper and Masataka Yoshida’s one-year, $18 million contract to the Pirates. His pitch rests on Cruz’s 2026 season.
“He hit 20 homers and stole 30 bags in 97 games,” Gordon said on WEEI’s Play Tessie podcast Wednesday.
Cruz, a 6-foot-7 left-handed hitter born Oct. 4, 1998, in Nizao, Dominican Republic, owns a career .243/.322/.438 line with 80 homers and 103 steals in 476 games since his 2021 debut. He hit .280/.368/.486 in 97 games in 2026, good for 2.8 WAR, and missed time with non-displaced fractures in the metacarpals of his left hand.
Keller, a 6-foot-3 right-hander born April 4, 1996, in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, was a second-round Pirates pick in 2014. He went 6-8 with a 5.29 ERA and a 1.37 WHIP over 115 2/3 innings in 22 starts this year amid shoulder issues. His career record stands at 48-73 with a 4.60 ERA. He signed a five-year, $77 million extension in 2024, leaving roughly $18 million for 2027 and $20 million for 2028.
Bennett, a 6-foot-6 lefty born Dec. 2, 2000, in Tulsa, Oklahoma, arrived from Washington for Luis Perales in December 2025 and debuted May 1. He went 9-7 with a 3.65 ERA and struck out 91 in 113 1/3 innings over 19 starts.
Duran, a speedy, 6-foot outfielder born Sept. 5, 1996, in Corona, California, and a 2018 Red Sox draft pick, made the 2024 All-Star team, and won the All-Star Game MVP award, while batting .285/.342/.492 with 21 homers and 34 steals. He slumped to .207/.266/.361 in 2026, with 20 homers and 21 steals in 151 games, and projects to earn about $11 million in arbitration.
Gasper, a 5-foot-9 switch-hitter born Oct. 11, 1995, in New Hampshire and drafted by the Yankees in 2018, hit .251/.357/.466 with 10 homers in 67 games.
Yoshida, born July 15, 1993, in Japan, signed a five-year, $90 million deal that expires after 2027. He batted .274/.347/.399 in 87 games this year.
Oneil Cruz’s Fit in the Boston Red Sox Lineup
Cruz saw fastballs on 49.5 percent of pitches during the best offensive season of his career, according to Gordon.
“Oneil Cruz is good at handling that velocity,” the podcaster said. Gordon identified high-velocity pitches as a Boston weakness, but cautioned that the sample covers roughly one season.
Co-host Pat Brown flagged the other side.
“He was first percentile in strikeout rate, second percentile in whiff rate. That’s adding a lot of downside with risk,” Brown said. Cruz posted a .676 OPS in 2025, and his .854 mark in 2026 sits well above his career .760.
Position is the larger question. Gordon ruled out shortstop and left the rest open. “Probably mostly an outfielder and a DH, but you’re getting him for the bat and what he can do for you offensively,” Gordon said.
Boston’s outfield already features Roman Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela and Wilyer Abreu, and Rafaela, Abreu and third baseman Caleb Durbin all won 2026 Rawlings Gold Glove awards. Cruz’s defensive metrics in center field have been mixed to negative. “He was horrific at shortstop,” Pat said. Sammy saw third base as the best fit, but Durbin holds that job. The designated hitter spot is the opening, and Yoshida and Gasper, the players who fill it now, are the players leaving under the “Play Tessie” trade pitch.
The rotation takes a hit as well.
“If he’s in the deal, he takes the Jake Bennett slot,” Gordon said of Keller.
“Your rotation probably will be downgraded a bit,” co-host Sammy James added. Keller does not replace Sonny Gray either. Gray became a free agent in October after going 18-5 with a 2.72 ERA and 169 innings, against Keller’s 5.29 ERA.
Oneil Cruz Trade Verdict for Boston Red Sox and Pirates
The Pirates shed about $38 million in Keller money and absorb Yoshida’s $18 million, a savings of roughly $20 million, Gordon and James calculated. Duran’s $11 million arbitration figure and Cruz’s projected $7 million shrink that gap.
“For a Major League Baseball team, that’s not that much. But the Pirates are only technically a Major League Baseball team,” James quipped.
Brown sees Pittsburgh pulling the trigger.
“They are so strapped for cash that they would take the hit on a potential Oneil Cruz return just to free up a little bit of money,” he said. Brown sees Boston declining.
“You trade Yoshida, but you basically added a year of Yoshida,” Brown said.
James had both teams saying no, though barely for Pittsburgh.
“It’s very close to the Pirates taking it,” Sammy said. Gordon agreed and pointed to Boston’s preferences.
“If you brought this straight to their front offices, they would both say, ‘Thanks, but no thanks,'” Gordo said. He added that the Red Sox need “more certainty when it comes to the bat we’re adding.”
The financial result favors Pittsburgh. The Pirates move Keller’s 2028 salary, and Boston extends its commitment through that season while giving up Bennett’s 3.65 ERA and years of control. Boston keeps prospects such as Franklin Arias and Payton Tolle, the hosts noted, and still gets a single high-variance bat. The offense improves only if Cruz repeats 2026. The defense gains little.

item.title: [MLB.com] Las razones para creer en el repunte ofensivo de Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
item.dc:creator: Manny Randhawa
item.description: Cada vez que el dominicano Vladimir Guerrero Jr. conecta un jonrón, hay algo único en su recorrido por las bases. item.content:encoded:
Cada vez que el dominicano Vladimir Guerrero Jr. conecta un jonrón, hay algo único en su recorrido por las bases. Ocurre mientras se prepara para doblar por la tercera almohadilla, y se le conoce como el "paso de Vladdy".
Tiene un ritmo específico. Ayuda el hecho de que Vlad es un buen bailarín: la cadencia del paso le da el efecto deseado, un floreo final mientras se prepara para recorrer los últimos 90 pies de su más reciente trote jonronero.
Desafortunadamente para Guerrero y los Azulejos, no hubo muchos "pasos de Vladdy" en el 2026. De hecho, el seis veces convocado al Juego de Estrellas tuvo la peor temporada ofensiva de su carrera, terminando con una línea de .260/.332/.356 y apenas nueve bambinazos en 609 visitas al plato. No fue hasta mediados de septiembre que conectó su primer cuadrangular de la campaña en el Rogers Centre.
El abrupto declive de Guerrero fue una de las razones principales por las que Toronto le siguió a una campaña del 2025 en la que ganaron el banderín -- que puso a los Azulejos a dos outs de un título de Serie Mundial y generó aspiraciones de regresar al Clásico de Otoño en el 2026 -- con un último lugar en el Este de la Liga Americana.
De todas las interrogantes que enfrentan los Azulejos en este receso de temporada, esta es quizás la mayor, porque parece que como le va a Vlad, le va a los Azulejos colectivamente: ¿Logrará repuntar el rostro de la franquicia y su contrato de US$500 millones?
He aquí un vistazo a por qué hay motivos para creer que Guerrero recuperará su nivel:
Más tiempo para bailar
Guerrero perdió su ritmo ofensivo la temporada pasada. Tuvo un buen comienzo -- aunque sin su poder característico -- durante el primer mes. A finales de abril, había producido una línea de bateo de .354/.438/.469. La falta de poder (dos jonrones en ese lapso) ciertamente levantó sospechas, pero, a fin de cuentas, sólo había transcurrido un mes de campaña.
Luego, las cosas se... desincronizaron. Y para Guerrero, cuya mecánica en el plato involucra un ritmo meticuloso con un toque de la punta del pie y una delicada transferencia de peso, eso puede ser un desastre.
Pregúntenle a otro gran primera base toletero de la época reciente: Joey Votto. Votto publicó en las redes sociales en agosto que sentía que uno de los problemas de Guerrero esta pasada campaña fue que "su movimiento hacia adelante está retrasando que la maceta del bate encaje en su lugar".
En otras palabras, Guerrero tendió a irse hacia adelante más en el 2026, en lugar de mantener su peso apoyado en la pierna trasera hasta el momento preciso para transferirlo hacia el frente y usar su pie delantero para crear fuerza con el suelo. A menudo, esto resultó en batazos rodados.
En el baile, deslizarse o balancearse es algo que haces a propósito. En el plato, no tanto.
"[Guerrero] es un atleta y bateador tan dinámico que es un problema realmente complejo", indicó el gerente general de los Azulejos, Ross Atkins. "Probablemente todos aquí puedan emular su ritmo y tiempo, ese toque de la punta del pie y cómo crea ese impulso. Es algo realmente impresionante de ver".
"A medida que perdió un poco de ese ritmo y sincronización al principio de la temporada, comenzó a afectar su confianza. Una vez que impactó su confianza, los ajustes durante el juego y la campaña se volvieron muy difíciles".
Ahí radica el problema cuando estás fuera de sincronía en el plato durante la temporada: es difícil hacer ajustes sobre la marcha. Siempre hay otro juego al día siguiente. Ahora que es el receso de campaña, Guerrero finalmente tiene tiempo para respirar. En términos de ritmo en el plato, por fin puede "bailar" ininterrumpidamente de nuevo.
En junio, con Guerrero sumido en lo que se convertiría en el peor mes de su carrera (OPS de .498), dijo que sentía que pronto iba a encenderse. Pero lo que expresó también subrayó la dificultad de hacer ajustes durante la campaña: no se puede hacer más de lo posible.
"Me he estado sintiendo bien y le he estado dando con fuerza a la bola", declaró Guerrero. "No hay nada que pueda hacer, solo trato de salir y darle un buen swing a la pelota. Le he estado pegando fuerte últimamente, pero esto es béisbol. Voy a seguir trabajando duro y seguir haciendo esto".
Ver para creer
Tras su decepcionante campaña del 2026, Guerrero decidió someterse a una cirugía ocular con láser para agudizar su visión, realizándose el procedimiento en el Laser Eye Center de Miami poco después del final de la temporada regular.
Otros jugadores de Grandes Ligas también se han sometido al procedimiento durante sus carreras, incluyendo al excompañero de equipo de Guerrero, Bo Bichette.
Antes de la cirugía, Guerrero usaba lentes de contacto durante los juegos. ¿Ayudará la cirugía láser? Bueno, probablemente no haga daño.
El sonido de un contacto sólido es música para los oídos
Como señaló nuestro compañero Mike Petriello justo antes de la pausa del Juego de Estrellas, la inexplicable falta de poder de Guerrero no se debió a una mala suerte desmesurada, sino al hecho de que no estaba conectando la bola con la maceta del bate con tanta frecuencia (su tasa de barrels del 6.9% la temporada pasada, la más baja de su carrera, fue poco más de la mitad de lo que registró en el 2025: 12.2%) y su tasa de batazos fuertes se redujo significativamente (del 50.7% en el 2025 al 44.3% en el 2026). Cuando Guerrero sí le dio con fuerza a la pelota, frecuentemente fue por el suelo.
Cuando el ritmo y la sincronización de una secuencia mecánica en el plato están fuera de lugar, todo eso puede ocurrir.
¿Se necesitará de un receso de temporada para recalibrar y una visión más aguda en el plato a más batazos sólidos?
Y luego está la pregunta a nivel macro: ¿Quién es Vladimir Guerrero Jr. en el plato? ¿Es el Vlad del 2021, que conectó 48 jonrones y terminó segundo en la votación al JMV de la Liga Americana? ¿El mismo Vlad que aterrorizó al pitcheo rival durante la postemporada del 2025, cuando tuvo slugging de .795 con ocho bambinazos? ¿O es el Vlad de la temporada pasada, que registró slugging de .356?
A menudo, la respuesta a una pregunta como esa es: ninguna de las dos; en algún punto intermedio. Pero es poco probable que el Guerrero del 2026 sea el que veamos en el futuro.
No todo fue malo
La falta de poder es el tema principal. Y Guerrero tiene trabajo por hacer. Pero su campaña del 2026 sí tuvo algunos aspectos positivos:
Su tasa de ponches se mantuvo en la élite:
A lo largo de su carrera, Guerrero ha reducido constantemente su tasa de ponches. Fue buena para empezar (se ponchó en el 16.4% de sus visitas al plato durante sus primeras cuatro temporadas) pero en los últimos tres años, ha estado por debajo del 14%. La campaña pasada, fue del 13.3%, la más baja de su carrera y se ubicó entre el 8% de los mejores bateadores. (Aunque cabe señalar que persiguió pitcheos fuera de la zona mucho más de lo habitual, con una tasa de chase del 30.6% en el 2026, un tope personal).
La tasa de whiff (swings en blanco) del 20.1% de Guerrero durante la temporada del 2026 fue la más baja de su carrera y se ubicó en el percentil 76. El problema no fue el contacto.
Sigue teniendo uno de los bates más rápidos del juego:
La velocidad promedio del bate de Guerrero de 76.3 mph se ubicó en el percentil 92 entre los bateadores calificados la temporada pasada, y estuvo bastante cerca de lo que fue durante el año anterior (76.7). El problema no fue la velocidad del swing.
De regreso a la pista de baile
Será fascinante ver cómo se desempeña Guerrero la próxima vez que lo veamos en la caja de bateo durante un juego.
Si el ritmo y la fluidez en su mecánica en el plato regresan, Vladdy también estará de vuelta.
Después de todo, es demasiado bueno para que su producción por debajo del promedio continúe indefinidamente. Y él mismo te lo dirá, tal como lo hizo ante los reporteros en junio.
"Las cosas van a salir a mi manera", afirmó Guerrero. "En algún momento, el béisbol será bueno conmigo".

item.title: [MLB.com] How Vladdy can get his groove back in '27
item.dc:creator: Manny Randhawa
item.description: There’s a specific rhythm to it. It helps that Vlad is a good dancer -- the cadence of the shuffle gives it the desired effect: a final flourish as he prepares to travel the final 90 feet of his latest home run trot. Unfortunately for Guerrero and the Blue Jays, there weren’t many Vladdy shuffles in 2026. In fact, the six-time All-Star had the poorest offensive season of his career, finishing with a .260/.332/.356 slash line and just nine homers in 609 plate appearances. It wasn't until mid-Sept
item.content:encoded:
There’s a specific rhythm to it. It helps that Vlad is a good dancer -- the cadence of the shuffle gives it the desired effect: a final flourish as he prepares to travel the final 90 feet of his latest home run trot.
Unfortunately for Guerrero and the Blue Jays, there weren’t many Vladdy shuffles in 2026. In fact, the six-time All-Star had the poorest offensive season of his career, finishing with a .260/.332/.356 slash line and just nine homers in 609 plate appearances. It wasn't until mid-September that he hit his first home run of the season at Rogers Centre.
Guerrero’s sharp decline was a major reason Toronto followed up a pennant-winning 2025 campaign that brought the Blue Jays two outs from a World Series title and led to aspirations of a return to the Fall Classic in '26, with a last-place finish in the American League East.
Of all the questions the Blue Jays face this offseason, this one is perhaps the biggest, because it seems that as Vlad goes, so go the Jays collectively: Will the club’s $500 million face of the franchise rebound?
Here’s a look at why there’s reason to believe Guerrero will get his groove back:
More time to dance
Guerrero lost his rhythm offensively last season. He got off to a red-hot start -- albeit without his signature power -- over the first month. At the end of April, he had produced a .354/.438/.469 slash line. The power outage (two homers in that span) was certainly eyebrow-raising, but hey, it was only one month into the season.
Then, things got … out of sync. And for Guerrero, whose mechanics at the plate involve meticulous timing with a toe tap and delicate weight transfer, that can spell disaster.
Ask another great slugging first baseman of recent vintage -- Joey Votto. Votto posted on social media in August that he felt one of Guerrero's issues this past season was that "his forward move is delaying his barrel from snapping in place."
In other words, Guerrero tended to drift forward more in 2026, rather than keeping his weight stacked on his back leg until precisely the right moment for transferring his weight forward and using his lead foot to create force with the ground. It often resulted in balls pounded into the ground.
In dance, drifting or swaying is something you do on purpose. At the plate, not so much.
“[Guerrero]'s such a dynamic athlete and hitter that it’s a really complex problem,” Blue Jays general manager Ross Atkins said. “Everyone in here can probably emulate his rhythm and tempo, that toe tap and how he creates that momentum. It’s a really impressive thing to watch.
“As he lost a little bit of that rhythm and timing pretty early in the season, it started to impact his confidence. Once it impacted his confidence, the in-game adjustments and in-season adjustments became very difficult.”
Therein lies the problem when you’re out of whack at the plate during the season: it’s difficult to make adjustments on the fly. There’s always another game tomorrow. Now that it’s the offseason, Guerrero finally has time to breathe. In terms of rhythm at the plate, he can finally “dance” uninterrupted again.
Back in June, with Guerrero mired in what would become the single worst month of his career (.498 OPS), he said that he felt he was going to get hot soon. But what he said also underscored the difficulty of making in-season adjustments -- all you can do is all you can do.
“I’ve been feeling good and I’ve been hitting the ball hard,” Guerrero said. “There’s nothing I can do, I just try to go out there and put a good swing on the ball. I’ve been hitting the ball hard lately, but this is baseball. I’m going to keep working hard and keep doing this.”
Seeing is believing
Following his disappointing 2026 campaign, Guerrero decided to undergo laser eye surgery to sharpen his eyesight, having the procedure performed at the Laser Eye Center of Miami shortly after the end of the regular season.
The sound of a barrel is music to the ears
As our own Mike Petriello pointed out just prior to the All-Star break, Guerrero’s inexplicable power outage wasn’t due to inordinate bad luck, but rather the fact that he wasn’t barreling the ball nearly as often (his career-low 6.9% barrel rate last season was not much more than half of what it was in 2025 -- 12.2%) and his hard-hit rate was down significantly (from 50.7% in 2025, to 44.3% in ’26). When Guerrero did hit the ball hard, it was frequently on the ground.
When the rhythm and timing of a mechanical sequence at the plate are off, all of that can certainly happen.
Will an offseason to recalibrate and sharper vision at the plate lead to more barrels?
And then there's the macro question: Who is Vladimir Guerrero Jr. at the plate? Is he the 2021 Vlad, who smashed 48 homers and finished runner-up in AL MVP voting? The same Vlad who terrorized opposing pitching during the 2025 postseason, when he slugged .795 with eight homers? Or is he last season’s Vlad, who slugged .356?
Often, the answer to a question like that is: neither; somewhere in between. But it’s unlikely that 2026 Guerrero is the one we see going forward.
It wasn’t all bad
The missing power is the thing. And Guerrero has work to do. But his 2026 campaign did have some silver linings:
His strikeout rate remained elite:
Throughout his career, Guerrero has steadily lowered his strikeout rate. It was good to begin with -- he struck out in 16.4% of his plate appearances over his first four Major League seasons -- but over the past three years, it’s been below 14%. Last season, it was 13.3%, the lowest of his career and ranked among the top 8% of batters.
(Although it should be noted here that he chased a lot more than he usually does, with a career-high 30.6% chase rate in 2026.)
Guerrero’s 20.1% whiff rate during the 2026 campaign was the lowest of his career and ranked in the 76th percentile.
The problem wasn’t contact.
He still has one of the game’s fastest bats:
Guerrero’s average bat speed of 76.3 mph ranked in the 92nd percentile among qualified batters last season, and it was fairly close to what it was during the prior year (76.7).
The problem wasn’t swing speed.
Getting back on the dance floor
It will be fascinating to see how Guerrero performs the next time we see him in the batter’s box during a game.
If the rhythm and flow to his plate mechanics are back, Vladdy will be back, too.
After all, he’s too good for his subpar production to continue indefinitely. And he’ll tell you that, as he did reporters in June.
“Things are going to go my way,” Guerrero said. "At one point, the baseball is going to be good to me.”

item.content:encoded:
3 Best MLB Free Agent Fits For Seiya Suzuki If He Leaves Cubs
Power. Lots and lots of power.
That's what one is getting if they sign Chicago Cubs right fielder and designated hitter Seiya Suzuki, who's arguably the biggest power threat on the MLB free agent market this winter. Plus, the 32-year-old Suzuki is coming off quite possibly the best all-around season of his MLB career, offering both a respectable defensive presence in right field and a potent threat from the right side of the plate.
Here are the three best MLB free agent fits for Suzuki should he depart Chicago:
Simply put: The Cincinnati Reds need a right fielder.
The Reds continue to struggle to get consistent production from their outfield and offense as a whole. Plus, the Eugenio Suárez reunion didn't live up to the hype in 2026, as he finished with a mere .212/.307/.433 slash line while splitting time at the hot corner and designated hitter, and is now a free agent.
Suzuki would presumably become Cincinnati's starting right fielder, adding veteran assurance and an impactful veteran complement. Suzuki's electric bat would boost a Reds' offense that was last in MLB in hits (1,231) and on-base percentage (.305), 27th in runs (666) and 25th in slugging percentage (.394) last season.
Prior to 2026, Suzuki was Chicago's primary designated hitter in 2025 before making 110 starts and 111 appearances altogether in right field last season. On that front, Suzuki posted a career-high 5.1 wins above replacement while also logging 14 defensive runs.
Now, Cincinnati may want Héctor Rodríguez to be its everyday right fielder. In that case, Suzuki opens the season as the Reds' designated hitter and moves to right field if Rodríguez struggles or injury presents itself. While the Reds were fourth in the sport with 213 home runs last season, they need the offense, and Suzuki would provide a major lift in that regard.
What could stop the Reds — who finished in last place in the National League Central with 75 wins last season — from making a push for Suzuki, though, is them potentially feeling they're not close enough to contending for the playoffs to be doling out a potential nine-figure contract. Rather, they may hope that Rodríguez emerges as a building block and be cost-effective in filling out the rest of their depth chart.
The Texas Rangers need some oomph, which is precisely what Suzuki would provide.
Just one year ago in 2025, Suzuki, who boasts a career .472 slugging percentage and a 128 OPS+, totaled 32 home runs and 103 RBIs, both career highs. Suzuki would enhance a Texas offense that was just 25th in runs (673), 23rd in hits (1,296) and tied for 21st in slugging percentage (.396) last season.
As for Suzuki's potential fit with the Rangers, designated hitter Joc Pederson is a free agent, which would be the easiest way to slide Suzuki into the mix. Concurrently, right fielder Brandon Nimmo has the versatility and experience playing all three outfield positions should Texas want to play Suzuki in right field.
While Evan Carter is a commendable center fielder, he continues to struggle at the plate (Carter hit .194 across 455 plate appearances in 2026), creating a scenario where Texas could either move Wyatt Langford from left to center field or put Nimmo in center field, with Suzuki taking over in right field.
Either way, the Rangers — who, aside from Langford, have been unable to get their touted young position players to progress as hitters — need more slugging, and they have the wiggle room to add to their outfield rotation.
The Houston Astros won the American League West with a .500 record, edging out the Rangers by one game. It's reasonable to think the Rangers' starting rotation — a unit that led MLB with a 3.41 ERA in 2025 — will bounce back in 2027. With that in mind, a slightly improved offense could literally be all they need to win the AL West.
All that said, Texas may prefer to retain Pederson, who hit 26 home runs and posted a .487 slugging percentage in 2026, on a short-term deal to be its designated hitter and avoid switching gears with who plays where in the outfield.
At face value, the Atlanta Braves don't have a burning need for a right fielder. When putting a magnifying glass closer to the object at hand, though, signing Suzuki would be a slick move.
For starters, the Braves were muzzled by the Los Angeles Dodgers — who were then swept by the Milwaukee Brewers in the NL Championship Series — in the NL Division Series, tallying just eight runs and 18 hits across the would-be four-game series. Meanwhile, versatile left fielder Mauricio Dubón, outfielder and midseason pickup Lane Thomas and designated hitter/first baseman Dominic Smith are free agents.
Adding a considerable hitter who's also a body for the outfield mix would be timely.
Suzuki represents a defensive alternative to Ronald Acuña Jr., who has underwhelmed at the corner outfield position by his standards of late and made 14 starts as the team's designated hitter last season, and offers a way for the Braves to ease the homegrown star into being the team's DH on a more consistent basis, if wanted.
Plus, the combination of a torn ACL, as well as calf and hamstring issues, have limited Acuña to just 251 regular games since the outset of the 2023 MLB season. Adding another All-Star-caliber outfielder to the mix warrants consideration from a health standpoint, alone.
Suzuki would fit Atlanta's timeline as an NL contender with a core of players who are primarily in their prime.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Tarik Skubal Can’t Fix What Keeps Costing the Yankees
item.dc:creator: Jonna Perlinger; Unknown
item.description: The New York Yankees are reportedly among the potential suitors for Tarik Skubal, but just because they can pursue one of baseball's best pitchers doesn't mean they should. The two-time American League Cy Young Award winner would strengthen virtually any rotation. item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are reportedly among the potential suitors for Tarik Skubal, but just because they can pursue one of baseball's best pitchers doesn't mean they should.
The two-time American League Cy Young Award winner would strengthen virtually any rotation. However, his projected price tag is difficult to justify considering New York's existing pitching depth and the weaknesses that derailed its 2026 postseason.
The Yankees don't need another ace nearly as much as they need a more complete baseball team.
The Yankees already have baseball's best starting rotation
The Yankees finished the 2026 regular season with MLB's best starting rotation ERA (3.30). Their pitching staff followed with a 2.63 ERA across five postseason games, making it difficult to blame pitching for their early October exit.
Consider the starters already under team control heading into 2027:
| Pitchers | ERA |
|---|---|
| Cam Schlittler | 1.95 |
| Carlos Rodon | 2.67 |
| Max Fried | 2.80 |
| Ryan Weathers | 3.60 |
| Gerrit Cole | 3.61 |
| Will Warren | 3.95 |
Schlittler has emerged as one of baseball's most exciting young arms. The 25-year-old AL Cy Young finalist finished 2026 with 239 strikeouts across 193⅔ innings, a 0.92 WHIP and a 2.56 FIP.
Meanwhile, Fried, Rodon and Cole provide veteran experience, with Weathers and Warren offering additional depth.
The Yankees also have Carlos Lagrange, whose fastball can reach 103 mph. Although transitioned to relief during 2026, the organization still views him as a potential long-term starter.
Injuries and regression remain concerns, particularly with aging veterans. But with Warren, Weathers and Clarke Schmidt providing additional starting options, protecting against those possibilities doesn't require signing the market's most expensive pitcher.
Skubal's projected contract creates a difficult financial equation
According to ESPN's Kiley McDaniel, Skubal is projected to command an eight-year, $352 million contract, averaging $44 million annually.
That would surpass Max Scherzer's record $43.3 million annual average and Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million guarantee for a pitcher.
The Yankees already committed $324 million to Cole, $218 million to Fried and $162 million to Rodon. Adding Skubal would bring those four pitchers' combined original guarantees to approximately $1.06 billion.
Those contracts span different periods, but the figure illustrates how heavily New York would be investing in one area of its roster.
Skubal also turns 30 in November and has undergone multiple elbow procedures, including Tommy John surgery in college, flexor tendon surgery in 2022 and another procedure in 2026.
His talent isn't in question, but an eight-year commitment carries considerable risk.
There's also a longer-term financial consideration.
Cole and Rodon are under contract through 2028, meaning their combined $63 million in annual salaries is scheduled to come off New York's payroll before Paul Skenes could become available.
Skenes is projected to reach free agency following the 2029 season, potentially presenting the Yankees with another opportunity to pursue elite pitching when they're better positioned financially.
There's no guarantee Skenes reaches free agency or signs with New York. But his timeline illustrates the value of preserving flexibility rather than committing another $350 million to an already dominant rotation.
New York's past several postseasons have exposed problems another ace cannot fix
The Yankees' October struggles weren't caused by a lack of quality starting pitching.
They were caused by recurring weaknesses: defensive mistakes, inconsistent situational hitting and an inability to manufacture runs.
Against Tampa Bay, New York committed four errors in Game 2, including three in the opening inning behind Schlittler.
The offense also struggled to capitalize on scoring opportunities, reinforcing concerns about a lineup overly dependent on the long ball.
Those problems won't disappear because Skubal pitches every fifth day.
New York needs defensive reliability, greater lineup balance and hitters capable of producing runs without relying exclusively on home runs.
That's where Brian Cashman's attention should be focused.
The Yankees have more important places to spend their money
The most immediate concern is retaining David Bednar.
The two-time All-Star converted 35 of 39 save opportunities in 2026, posting a 2.47 ERA with 76 strikeouts across 69⅓ innings.
The Yankees extended Bednar a one-year, $23.15 million qualifying offer, but that doesn't guarantee his return.
With Bednar having until November 17 to accept or decline, New York could still find itself competing for his services on the open market. Without an established replacement, securing a dependable closer should take precedence over adding another expensive starter.
Bullpen depth is another priority, particularly with left-handers Tim Hill and Ryan Yarbrough reaching free agency.
Then there's the infield.
The Yankees need greater production and defensive consistency at second and third base, along with a right-handed bat to balance their lineup. Catching depth and outfield stability also warrant attention.
Addressing those weaknesses through offensive upgrades, infield improvements and bullpen reinforcements would do more to balance the roster than investing another $44 million annually in starting pitching.
Even if signing Skubal allowed New York to trade from its pitching surplus, those deals would need to deliver meaningful improvements elsewhere to justify the investment.
The Yankees have already invested heavily in their rotation, developed an emerging ace in Schlittler and assembled the league's best starting staff.
Now they need to build a better team around it.
Another $350 million pitcher might make headlines. Addressing the weaknesses that keep costing the Yankees in October would make considerably more sense.
Jonna Perlinger's love for baseball began long before Yankees manager Buck Showalter handed her a broken bat at six years old, but that moment helped shape a lifelong passion for the game and the Bronx Bombers. She serves as Baseball Content Lead, Lead Yankees Writer, and Director of Social Media for On New Jersey Sports (ONNJ), and is the founder of Babe's Babes Media, an independent, women-led baseball platform established in 2023. Her reporting has taken her to some of baseball's biggest stages, including the World Baseball Classic, MLB All-Star Week, Winter Meetings, and Men's College World Series. Jonna has a deep appreciation for baseball's history and traditions, and a passion for telling the stories of the people who make the game special, both on and off the field.
Follow 90syankskid

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Cubs free agent target: Tarik Skubal
item.dc:creator: Al Yellon
item.description: It's that time of year again, with the 2026 season in the books. Free agent season! Only this year, it's different, because only a few weeks from now, MLB owners are likely going to lock out MLB players and all transactions, along with everything else in MLB, will stop. item.content:encoded:
It's that time of year again, with the 2026 season in the books. Free agent season!
Only this year, it's different, because only a few weeks from now, MLB owners are likely going to lock out MLB players and all transactions, along with everything else in MLB, will stop. This could lead to a lot of signings over the next few weeks, as I noted in this article last month.
In this series I'm going to look at some players who the Cubs could target in free agency, guys who could be useful to the team in different areas. I've already done that for the Cubs' own free agents in this series from last month. For this series I'm going to be working off of MLB Trade Rumors' Top 50 free agent list, though I won't write about absolutely everyone on the list.
So, Tarik Skubal. Clearly the top free-agent pitcher, clearly one of the best pitchers in baseball. He turns 30 in a couple of weeks and has had three outstanding seasons in a row, after missing some of the 2023 season with elbow issues. (He also had some of those this year, but came back from a "loose bodies" elbow procedure with no apparent ill effects.)
Various sources have projected him to get a contract between eight and 10 years with a total value of $350 million to $500 million. MLBTR says nine years, $425 million, or an AAV of $47.2 million.
Let's stop right here. You know the Cubs aren't going to do that. I know the Cubs aren't going to do that.
I'm here to argue that the Cubs shouldn't do that, even if they could.
Well, that's provocative. Let me explain.
All five of the pitchers in the Cubs' rotation at the end of the 2026 season — Shōta Imanaga, Kevin Gausman, David Peterson, Clay Holmes and Matthew Boyd — are free agents. Beyond that, the next-up group, Ben Brown, Cade Horton and Justin Steele, all had various forms of injuries in 2026 and what they can contribute in 2027 is uncertain.
So that leaves… Javier Assad and what army?
With Skubal expected to get an AAV of at least $40 million and perhaps $50 million, what would that leave for the Cubs to sign other pitchers? Skubal can't pitch every game.
Should the Cubs spend that much on free-agent pitchers (or on those they acquire by trade)? Absolutely, positively yes. They need to invest in pitching infrastructure and stop trying to patch the sinking ship, as they did this year. And in my view, the best way to do that — if they're going to invest $50 million in that infrastructure this winter — would be to use it on multiple pitchers. Guys who might not be Cy Young candidates, but maybe No. 2 guys. I'll talk about some of those guys in upcoming installments in this series.
Maybe you don't agree with me or believe me. Maybe you'll believe ESPN's Jeff Passan:
The Chicago Cubs badly want Skubal. They also are skeptical that they will be willing to compete at the sort of dollars Skubal is expected to get — well in excess of $300 million, potentially in the $400 million-plus range.
And that's exactly my point. The Cubs don't have to sign the guy who makes the most money to succeed. In fact, they did spend quite a bit of money last offseason on Alex Bregman, and after a slow start for the third baseman, that worked out just fine.
If the Cubs do want to compete, spread out that money over multiple pitchers. Don't put it all on one guy.
I'm sure you'll tell me why I'm wrong, so have at it. But my stance is: Pass on Skubal. Spend the money? Absolutely. Just do it elsewhere.

item.content:encoded:
If you’re among the crowd that laments the way the Cubs have treated Javier Assad over the last few years, this latest bit of news isn’t going to make you feel any better. The righty bounced between Chicago and Triple-A Iowa again this past season despite all the big club’s pitching woes because he still had a minor-league option available. And while his underlying metrics indicate that he should have been awful, Assad managed to pitch competently once again.
Just not competently enough for the club to pick up his $3.3 million option for 2027, as MLB.com’s Jordan Bastian reported. Assad is still arbitration-eligible, however, so he remains under club control through 2028 at whatever salary that process determines. And based on MLB Trade Rumors’ projections, that should be just shy of $2 million for this coming season. That’s a very modest raise over the $1.8 million figure he earned for 2026.
I won’t argue with you about that being kind of a cheap move, though it’s not quite on par with Mr. Shirley eliminating Christmas bonuses in favor of a subscription to the Jelly of the Month Club. But if you’re among those who believe Assad is the gift that keeps on giving the whole year at Clark and Addison, I’ll caution you to look a little closer at those results.
Assad’s ERA has always been much better than his FIP, which wouldn’t be as much of a concern if he wasn’t in the first percentile among his peers in both chase and whiff rate. He’s among the bottom 10% in strikeout rate, and his hard-hit rate is just barely above that. Some wonder why he’s not being given more chances; I wonder how he’s been able to get away with this for so long.
My argument is that Assad’s limited usage is precisely why he’s been decent in spite of what the data says. The Cubs know that, which is why they’re being “cheap” in this instance. And if all goes well, Jed Hoyer will add enough pitching that Assad won’t be needed in the rotation next season.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox got off to a disappointing 10-17 start in 2026, leading the organization to part ways with manager Alex Cora and several members of his coaching staff.
Boston's season ultimately ended in the American League Wild Card Series against the rival New York Yankees. After the season, the Red Sox removed the interim tag from Chad Tracy and officially named him their new manager, signing him to a three-year contract that runs through the 2029 season.
While Cora is still looking for his next Major League Baseball job, one former Boston staffer who was let go alongside him has resurfaced and will remain in the American League.
The Tigers Are Hiring Former Boston Red Sox Third Base Coach Kyle Hudson
As initially reported by Boston beat writer Rob Bradford, the Tigers are hiring former Red Sox third base coach Kyle Hudson as the official replacement for Anthony Sanders.
"Per sources, former Red Sox third base coach Kyle Hudson will be the Tigers new first base coach," Bradford wrote on X, formerly known as Twitter.
Additionally, Tigers beat writer Chris McCosky confirmed the news from Detroit's side of things, writing the following update:
"Confirming reports that Kyle Hudson, former Red Sox third base coach, has been hired by the Tigers as their new first base coach for 2027, replacing Anthony Sanders."
Before being relieved of his duties along with Cora, Hudson had spent three-plus years in Boston.
Kyle Hudson Resurfaces With The Tigers
The Baltimore Orioles took Hudson in the fourth round of the 2008 MLB Draft, and he reached the majors three years later. He made his MLB debut in September 2011 but was released the following January.
Hudson spent portions of the 2012 season in the organizations of the Texas Rangers, Tampa Bay Rays and Philadelphia Phillies before returning to Baltimore in 2013. He appeared in 103 games for Double-A Bowie that year, hitting .292 and stealing 26 bases.
After brief stops with the Los Angeles Angels and Dodgers organizations, Hudson shifted his focus to coaching. He served as the bench coach for Triple-A Columbus in 2019 before joining Cleveland's major league coaching staff the following season.
Hudson moved to Boston in 2023, initially serving as the Red Sox's first base coach and outfield instructor. He transitioned to third base coach in 2024 and remained in that role until the Red Sox dismissed him during their sluggish start to the 2026 season.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Fired Red Sox Coach Suddenly Resurfaces With New American League Club appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [yardbarker.com] Mets have question marks at several key positions
item.dc:creator: Bill Ladson
item.description: The New York Mets were able to get off to a good start this offseason when Bo Bichette exercised his $42 million option to stay with the club for the 2027 season. After a slow start, Bichette proved to be a valuable commodity, going 39-for-133 (.293) with runners in scoring position and holding his own at third base. New York, however, needs more than Bichette’s presence to improve from 2026, a season in which they won 73 games and failed to reach the postseason for the second consecutive year.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Mets were able to get off to a good start this offseason when Bo Bichette exercised his $42 million option to stay with the club for the 2027 season.
After a slow start, Bichette proved to be a valuable commodity, going 39-for-133 (.293) with runners in scoring position and holding his own at third base.
New York, however, needs more than Bichette’s presence to improve from 2026, a season in which they won 73 games and failed to reach the postseason for the second consecutive year. As they head into the GM meetings next week, here are the positions the Mets need to fix before Opening Day gets under way against the Marlins.
Decide on who is the starting catcher: It’s hard to believe the Mets are going into next season believing Francisco Alvarez is No. 1 behind the plate because Luis Torrens had a great season with the glove and showed improvement in the batter’s box. Torrens led the club in defensive runs saved (12) and had a slash line of .277/.351/ .523 with runners in scoring position. Thus far, Alvarez has been injury prone and recorded -5 defensive runs saved during his career.
First Base: For starters, the Mets made a mistake letting Pete Alonso walk and take his power production to the Orioles. With Alonso sent packing, the Mets used eight first basemen with Jared Young getting most of the playing time in '26. Young played well under manager Andy Green, but is Young an everyday player? Against left-handed pitching Young had a .228 batting average -- granted in limited at-bats. Defensively, Young was more than adequate, recording a 2 in defensive runs saved. Keep in mind that Jake Bauers is a free agent after helping the Brewers win a World Series title, but is he worth getting a big contract after having one good season? Based on what he did in ‘26, Bauers had a high-on base percentage.
Second Base: Marcus Semien is 36 years old and it will be interesting to see how much he has left in the tank. Semien provided almost nothing on offense and defense this past season. In fact, Semien hasn’t had a productive season since 2023 when he helped the Rangers win the World Series title. He may need to compete for a starting job this coming spring. Maybe a platoon between Semien and Brett Baty may help the club. Baty, who played 184 innings at the position, was slashing .250/.318/.406 with 11 homers against right-handed pitching in '27.
Closer: The Mets saw Devin Williams and Kodai Senga close games, but neither was consistent during the ninth inning. While Senga loved being the ninth inning guy towards the end of the season, he would like to return to rotation. One has to ask, Can Williams handle playing in New York? In his two years in the Big Apple (one year each with the Yankees and Mets), Williams has been a bust and has two years left on his contract.
Designated hitter: On paper, Jorge Polanco is the everyday DH. Really? Year 1 of that two-year, $40 million contract for Polanco didn’t go well. On April 18, Polanco went on the 10-day Injured List because of a right wrist contusion and left Achilles bursitis. While the wrist problems went away, the Achilles problems didn’t. By late August, Polanco had season-ending surgery on the Achilles. If Polanco is not ready for next season, Mark Vientos could be the guy. The Mets are still looking for him to work his magic at the plate like he did in 2024, when he hit a career-high 27 homers.
Veteran starter: They started the season with the hope that Freddy Peralta and Clay Holmes would lead the rotation, but they were both dealt to the Rays and Cubs, respectively, before the MLB Trade Deadline. The Mets are still looking for the 2024 version of Sean Manaea to show up. It was another year of inconsistency on the mound for him. New York currently has a young rotation led by Nolan McLean. Because of the Mets' reputation of spending money, there are going to be reports about them being involved in the Tarik Skubal sweepstakes. Other than Skubal and maybe Holmes, the free agents class in the starting pitching category is below average. The Mets more than likely will have to make a trade to acquire that arm.

item.title: [roundtable.io] Bryce Harper Named Phillies Top Trade Asset Entering Offseason
item.dc:creator: Matt Levine
item.description: The Phillies have some tough decisions to make this winter. After a poor September stretch of games, the Phillies barely reached the postseason as the final wild-card team in the National League. Philadelphia then was bounced by the Atlanta Braves, sending them to an early offseason. As the team heads into a crucial offseason, there could be some big changes coming to the roster. Philadelphia has already decided to bring back manager Don Mattingly for the upcoming season, adding some continuity
item.content:encoded:
The Phillies have some tough decisions to make this winter.
After a poor September stretch of games, the Phillies barely reached the postseason as the final wild-card team in the National League. Philadelphia then was bounced by the Atlanta Braves, sending them to an early offseason.
As the team heads into a crucial offseason, there could be some big changes coming to the roster. Philadelphia has already decided to bring back manager Don Mattingly for the upcoming season, adding some continuity to the team.
But after another poor ending to the year, the Phillies could elect to make some decisions around the team. The core of the roster is still very good, but something has to change with this unit to get over the hump of winning the World Series.
One of those could come around star Bryce Harper, who put together a very nice season for the Phillies. Harper is getting up there in age, now at 34, and the Phillies could elect to gauge the trade market for the veteran slugger.
In a new article from MLB analyst Zachary D. Rymer of Bleacher Report, Harper is listed as the team's top trade asset. There have been rumors about a trade of Harper from the Phillies in the past, but up to this point, the team has held back.
But following another early playoff exit, it could finally take place this offseason, especially with the impending lockout coming. Teams won't know what the financial implications of a new CBA will be, and moving off the large contract of Harper could make sense.
Multiple teams would be interested in going after Harper if the Phillies made him available. And the team could net a large haul for the star slugger, even at his age.
While it seems unlikely for the Phillies to make this move, it could still happen, especially given the relationship that Harper has had with the organization in the past. Phillies president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski and Harper have seen their share of issues
In all likelihood, Harper will be back with the Phillies for 2027 and beyond, but if the team wanted to make a major change, moving him could make some sense. Philadelphia wants to win a World Series, and the moves made this offseason could determine a lot for the next few years of the franchise.
