item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees had another very strong regular season where they went 93-68 in 161 games.
That said, they also had another letdown in the MLB playoffs when they got swept by the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS.
In addition, the Yankees also lost the final game on their home field in the Bronx.
Yankees Star Makes 6-Word Aaron Boone Statement
With their season over, a lot of blame has been placed on manager Aaron Boone.
They have only been able to reach the World Series one time over his nine-year stint as manager.
In a recent interview with Michael Kay (via The Michael Kay Show), José Caballero was asked about Boone.
Kay: “Did you like playing for Aaron Boone?”
Caballero: “Hey, I like playing for him. I like playing for the Yankees. I think we are, like I say, a complete team that we could do way better than what we did. And like I said, I think there’s no one else to blame than us as players. We were in there, we the ones making plays and hitting the ball.”
Looking At Boone
Manager Aaron Boone #17 of the New York Yankees walks out to the mound during the fifth inning against the Tampa Bay Rays in game two of the American League Division Series at Tropicana Field on October 05, 2026 in St Petersburg, Florida.
Boone took over the Yankees in 2018.
They have made the MLB playoffs in eight out of his nine seasons (and reached Game 5 of the 2024 World Series).
The Yankees wrote (via X) on February 20, 2025: “The New York Yankees today announced that they have signed Manager Aaron Boone to a two-year contract extension through the 2027 season.”
Looking At Caballero
Jose Caballero #72 of the New York Yankees reacts following his eighth inning three-run home run against the Boston Red Sox at Yankee Stadium on August 30, 2026 in New York City.
Caballero has been in the MLB for four seasons.
He spent the first year of his career with the Seattle Mariners.
Following Seattle, Caballero played part of two seasons for the Rays.
MLB.com wrote (on July 31, 2025): “Tampa Bay Rays traded SS José Caballero to New York Yankees for CF Everson Pereira and Future Considerations. Player To Be Named Later or Cash Considerations.”

item.content:encoded:
CLEVELAND –- José Ramírez se retirará entre los líderes en muchos departamentos de por vida en los Guardianes. De hecho, ya está primero en partidos jugados (1,734) y extrabases (765), más segundo en jonrones (297) – entre muchas cifras destacadas en la historia de la franquicia.
El sábado en el Juego 4 de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana, el dominicano empató un récord de Cleveland de más partidos consecutivos embasándose en la postemporada con 16, desde el 2024. El jardinero Steven Kwam tenía el récord, que ahora comparte con Ramírez, al hacer lo mismo entre el 2022 y el 2024.
“Mr. Lapara”, llegó el sábado a 16 juegos consecutivos embasándose en playoffs al negociar una base por bolas ante su compatriota y derecho de los Rays, Freddy Peralta, quien había entrado al partido como relevista. En total, Ramírez ha participado en ocho postemporadas con los Guardianes, también una marca de todos los tiempos del equipo.

Kyle Tucker, who was signed to a four-year, $240 million deal ahead of the 2026 season, addressed fans as the future of the franchise is in limbo. "Through every high and low, thank you to our fans for riding with us all season. We
item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers face several questions after an early postseason exit in the National League Championship Series.
The dynasty that the Dodgers have put together is in jeopardy of ending within the next few seasons if the front office can't assemble another winning roster. Kyle Tucker, who was signed to a four-year, $240 million deal ahead of the 2026 season, addressed fans as the future of the franchise is in limbo.
"Through every high and low, thank you to our fans for riding with us all season. We appreciate the love and support more than you know. This isn't the end — we'll be back," Tucker wrote in an Instagram post.
For most of 2026, the four-time All-Star was far from full form. Tucker ended the regular season with a .233 batting average, 17 home runs and 70 RBIs. He entered October with a .715 OPS, the lowest mark since his debut season in 2018 when he played 28 games.
Tucker's struggles became a point of contention among the fan base, but the star outfielder came to life in the postseason. The 29-year-old averaged .333 with a .967 OPS in October, which was perhaps the only highlight of his inaugural Dodgers season.
The Dodgers, who face an uncertain future after the failed quest for a three-peat, will need Tucker to play at All-Star strength the entire 2027 season as one of the many veterans on the roster. While Tucker's performance next year can't be known, one thing is certain, the Dodgers will surely try to get younger this winter.

item.content:encoded:
The San Diego Padres were able to get into the playoffs after what was a shaky start to the 2026 MLB season, but the team fell short of its goal to win the World Series.
San Diego lost in four games to the Milwaukee Brewers, seeing another year go by without a title, sending this team into a crucial offseason. The Padres' front office will have a lot to figure out this offseason, especially within the starting rotation, with key players hitting free agency.
Padres Linked With Tarik Skubal
One name that has started to generate some buzz around the Padres as the offseason gets going is ace Tarik Skubal, who split time with the Los Angeles Dodgers and Detroit Tigers. San Diego could look to go after Skubal, giving their rotation a major boost for the future.
MLB analyst Zachary D. Rymer of Bleacher Report recently ranked landing spots for Skubal in a new piece. Within this, Rymer listed the Padres as a top landing spot, and the fit does make a lot of sense.
"If ever there was a way to show they mean business, it's by signing Skubal away from those darn Dodgers. Maybe it wouldn't totally undo the little brother vs. big brother dynamic between the two NL West powers, but it would give the Padres a real trump card: the best pitcher in baseball.
"Besides, the Padres are going to need Skubal if Michael King declines his $28 million player option for 2027 and becomes a free agent. Skubal is one of the few pitchers in MLB who would represent an upgrade over King, even if signing him would likely cost more than $40 million per year," Rymer wrote.
The Padres have spent a lot of money in the last few offseasons, which has backfired on this franchise at times. It has seen the team allow multiple stars to leave town, pushing back what the ceiling of this organization could be.
Skubal could change the entire starting rotation for the Padres this offseason, but he is expected to receive a deal over $300 million, if not closer to $400 million. San Diego has given out large contracts in the past, but this would be a new precedent for this team.
Should the Padres Go After Tarik Skubal?
On the field, the Padres should absolutely do whatever it takes to bring Skubal to San Diego. But the money is will be another question that this organization is going to have to grapple with.
With the new ownership in place, the Padres are expected to keep spending, but giving Skubal what he wants could be tough. San Diego has a lot of heavy contracts on the books already, and handing out another could be a big swing for this team.
Overall, the Padres will be involved in the Skubal sweepstakes, especially with how president of baseball operations A.J. Preller operates. Nobody can count out San Diego in this process, but other teams could present an easier path to give the lefty ace the type of deal that he is looking for this winter.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Padres Predicted to Land Tarik Skubal in Blockbuster Offseason Move appeared first on HEAVY.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox's lefty-dominated starting rotation is expected to lose its only righty and its ace. Sonny Gray will take to the free agent market after he posted one of the best seasons of his career at age 36.
Gray has a mutual option on his contract, but those are rarely triggered. He and the Red Sox have to agree on his pay and $30 million is likely more than the front office is willing to commit for one year of the 37 year old Gray.
A reunion isn't completely off the table, though. Gray was discouraged with Red Sox manager Chad Tracy's to pull him in the fifth inning of Wild Card Game 2, but he has seemingly put that aside and mentioned Boston as a potential future destination when speaking about winning a championship before he retires (subscription required).
There are still some possible obstacles to a reunion between Gray and the Sox, though. MLB insider Mark Feinsand reports that the Red Sox will be among Gray's "primary suitors" this offseason, but some believe he might want to play for a team closer to his home in Tennessee.
MLB insider Mark Feinsand believes geography may come between Red Sox-Sonny Gray reunion
That belief makes sense, given the way Gray framed his comments on his potential retirement — he said he would be done with baseball "in a heartbeat" if his family wanted him to be. Proximity to them is obviously important to the veteran.
It is promising that the Red Sox are expected to be one of the teams pursuing Gray most aggressively. He was one of the best pitchers in the American League last season, likely to finish in or near the top five in Cy Young Award voting, and none of the righties the Red Sox already have are quite as promising. Brayan Bello had one of the strangest, up-and-down years we'll ever see and there's no guarantee of his performance next year. Tanner Houck and Kutter Crawford were injured all season and their futures are just as clouded.
If Gray is hoping to play his final seasons closer to his home, the Atlanta Braves could be dangerous competition in his market. Righty Tyler Mahle will be a free agent. Spencer Strider dealt with elbow inflammation for much of last season and he's regressed from his early career success. Spencer Schwellenbach missed the entire 2026 season due to injury. Given their 2026 performances, Gray might think he has a better chance of winning a championship with the Braves than with the Red Sox, furthering Atlanta's potential as a top suitor.
While improving the offense should undoubtedly be Boston's No. 1 priority this offseason, reuniting with Gray would be an undeniable boost to its rotation. If the Red Sox hope to keep him Gray in the northeast for another year or two, they'll have to outbid and outperform suitors local to Tennessee this winter.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees Center Field Dilemma Points To Oneil Cruz Trade
item.dc:creator: Pete Altomaro
item.description: The New York Yankees enter this offseason with a glaring hole in center field that free agency will not fill. The front office needs a solution now, but the available names on the market look weak. According to Yahoo Sports, the team simply does not have many options to sign as free agents. item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees enter this offseason with a glaring hole in center field that free agency will not fill. The front office needs a solution now, but the available names on the market look weak. According to Yahoo Sports, the team simply does not have many options to sign as free agents. This reality forces the club to look elsewhere for help.
Internal fixes have failed to work over the last two years. Austin Wells at catcher for example has shown great skills with his glove, but his bat has struggled to find a rhythm. The team also tried rookie Spencer Jones, who looked fresh but posted a minus-4 Outs Above Average metric in center field. That number was only a slight improvement over the minus-6 mark recorded by veteran Trent Grisham. Per Yahoo Sports, the defensive regression at this key position has become a major problem for the roster.
The Free Agent Trap
Most teams would look to the open market to fix a defensive gap. The Yankees cannot do that this time. The best available players come with heavy baggage. Daulton Varsho cannot hit well enough to justify the cost, and Luis Robert Jr. is known for being injury-prone while also lacking consistent offense. Even if Grisham returns, he should only play a corner spot, not center. Reports note that his glove has regressed since his bat finally improved in New York.
This lack of viable names means the Yankees must be creative. They cannot just wait for a deal to happen. The team needs to make a move that others might think is too risky. A trade is the only way to get a player who can actually play center field every day.
The Cruz Connection
Oneil Cruz stands out as the most logical target for this difficult task. He is a charismatic left-handed hitter who was named after Paul O'Neill. The Yankees have been linked to Cruz for years, with reports dating back to the summer of 2025. Nothing came of those talks then, but the interest never really went away. Yahoo Sports reports that the front office has targeted Cruz for a minimum of two years.
Getting him will not be easy. Reports suggest that the Pittsburgh Pirates might require some serious prying to part ways with their star. The Yankees have the assets to make a deal work, but they must act fast. Waiting too long could let another team step in and claim him. The clock is ticking on this specific opportunity to fix the roster.
Historical Context
The need for a true center fielder is not new for this franchise. Brett Gardner was probably the best the team had in the last 20 years before he retired after the 2021 season. A dropped fly ball during Game 5 of the 2024 World Series ended center field duties for Aaron Judge, despite his status as an elite player. The team has tried many names, but none have solved the issue for a full season.

CSPは、アスリートのトレーニングやパフォーマンス向上を専門とする施設で、野球選手の投球や打撃の分析も行っている。今永は2025年10月にも同施設を訪れ、投球分析を実施。MLB公式サイトが当時の取り組みを報じた。そして今回、CSPの創業者エリック・クレッシー氏が自身のYouTubeチャンネルで動画を公開。今永のトレーニングの様子を伝えている。

item.content:encoded:
Earlier this week, White Sox GM Chris Getz spoke to the media for the first time since Chicago’s ALDS Game 5 loss against the Guardians. Getz reflected on the season and provided some updates on the future. Among the topics of conversation were positions the White Sox will pursue upgrades in during the upcoming offseason, with Getz emphasizing the starting rotation as an obvious area of need. I previously discussed a few starting pitching options I’d like to see the White Sox pursue, so this will be a bit of a different conversation. Let’s discuss a dream target, a realistic target, and a mistake the White Sox could make in their pitching search.
Dream Target: LHP Tarik Skubal
It’s impossible to discuss the pitching free agent class without mentioning two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, the best pitcher available by a wide margin and one of the most dominant arms in all of baseball. The soon-to-be 30-year-old spent the first six and a half seasons with the Tigers before a midseason trade sent him to the Dodgers. He won the Cy Young Award in both 2024 and 2025, with a 2.39 and 2.21 ERA in each year, and would’ve been squarely in the mix for 2026 as well if not for an injury that cost him six weeks in May and June.
Do I think the White Sox have any chance at landing Tarik Skubal? Probably not. To be honest, I’d be surprised if they’re even interested. But Chicago has a very low payroll and an obvious need in the starting rotation. In theory, they could add Skubal for $30-40 million a year and still have payroll room for other upgrades on the roster. They’re a young, exciting team who seems to be just beginning their competitive window, so it’s a destination that could be appealing for Skubal. He’ll no doubt have his pick though, and it’s hard to see the White Sox competing financially with some of the other markets. I guess one can dream.
Realistic Target: RHP Tyler Mahle
Maybe big-game hunting isn’t realistic for the White Sox this offseason, but there’s no reason they can’t add at least one impact starting pitcher in free agency. Braves righty Tyler Mahle is an interesting veteran arm who shined during the second half of the season and into the playoffs. While most pitchers traded at the deadline struggled in their new home, Mahle posted a 1.99 ERA in nine starts with Atlanta and allowed just two earned runs in 13.1 innings in the Postseason. Mahle turned 32 in September and will be looking to leverage his strong finish into a solid contract. Perhaps a two or three-year deal could be in the cards for a player who’s always had a productive career but has battled frequent injuries. Mahle would be a strong veteran presence in the White Sox rotation and has a recent history of Postseason success. He could be one of the names on Chicago’s target list.
Mistake: LHP Robbie Ray
Left-hander Robbie Ray was one of the most talked about names ahead of the trade deadline, and the Giants ultimately dealt him within their division to the San Diego Padres. Some concerning metrics made Ray a prime candidate for regression, and he posted just a 5.02 ERA in nine starts for San Diego down the stretch. Still, he has back to back seasons with an ERA under 3.70, so he’s deserving of a big league deal this offseason. I don’t think that should be the White Sox, however. Ray is now 35 years old and his underlying metrics were scary in 2026. He pitched in two ballparks that heavily favor pitchers, whereas Chicago is a more hitter-friendly environment. Ray is a veteran who has struggled in the playoffs in his career, and his age is a real concern. I’d stay away here if I were the White Sox.

item.title: [fansided.com] The stars are aligning for the Mets to sign Tarik Skubal, with one giant asterisk standing in their way

item.content:encoded:
The offseason is a perfect time for New York Mets fans like myself to be optimistic, and that's exactly what I'm going to be doing here when I say the stars are aligning for the Mets to sign Tarik Skubal in free agency. I know, this seems crazy. Why would Skubal want to join a Mets team that just won 74 games in 2026 and has failed to make the playoffs in each of Juan Soto's two years in Flushing?
Well, here's a look at why the Mets make more sense for Skubal than you might think, and what might stand in their way of making this dream of arguably the best pitcher in the sport playing out the rest of his prime in Queens a reality.
The Dodgers' lack of aggression might play into the Mets' hands
When the Los Angeles Dodgers traded for Tarik Skubal, MLB fans not only assumed they'd automatically win a World Series title, but they also assumed that the Dodgers would easily extend Skubal, given their recent history of spending on star-level talent. It's absolutely possible that the Dodgers do choose to re-sign Skubal, but look at what ESPN's Alden Gonzalez had to say about that.
"Skubal's agent, Scott Boras, will probably want to get something done with his client before the lockout, but it would be really difficult for the Dodgers to justify signing Skubal to a massive deal before knowing what MLB's economic model will look like," Gonzalez wrote. "If there is a cap-and-floor system in the next collective bargaining agreement, there will be some sort of phase-in period. But it will undoubtedly impact the Dodgers in the near future. It would be a major risk to sign Skubal before knowing what they're signing up for."
To sum up, Gonzalez is predicting that Skubal's agent, Scott Boras, will likely want to get a deal done with his top client before the expected lockout at the beginning of December, but the Dodgers would want to wait until after the lockout so they know what the economic model of the sport will look like. This makes a ton of sense, given the massive amount of money they've already committed to 2027 and beyond. It's worth noting that this is just Gonzalez's belief, and not a sourced report.
If the Dodgers won't aggressively pursue Skubal before December 1, why can't the Mets be the team to give him an offer he can't refuse? It's not like the Mets haven't been in this position before.
The Mets have beaten the competition to the punch pre-lockout before
Just like a lockout is looming this offseason, one loomed back in the 2021 offseason, when Max Scherzer was a free agent. Scherzer, who was represented by Scott Boras, made it clear that he wanted to sign before the league locked the players out, and he did just that, coming to terms on a three-year, $130 milllion deal with, guess who, the New York Mets.
Now, say what you want about how the deal aged (Scherzer pitched brilliantly in 2022 but struggled in that year's postseason and was traded at the 2023 trade deadline), but the Mets beat the Dodgers and a couple of other teams to the punch to sign the future Hall of Famer on a deal that paid him well over $40 million annually.
Can't that history repeat itself? The Mets won the Scherzer sweepstakes not because they were some powerhouse, but because the Dodgers didn't want to go above and beyond to sign him as the Mets did. Reports suggest Skubal would like to sign pre-lockout and the Dodgers don't want to go above and beyond. Why can't the Mets do what they've already done and give their fan base something to get excited about before the lockout?
If the Dodgers and Mets won't pay Tarik Skubal, what team will?
Let's just assume that both the Dodgers and the Mets decide that paying Skubal is not in their best interest. Is there another team out there willing to spend the $300-to-$400 million on Skubal that he'll likely be asking for?
The New York Yankees are often willing spenders, but with a ton of money invested in starting pitchers like Gerrit Cole, Max Fried and Carlos Rodon, would they pay Skubal before addressing their offense? The Philadelphia Phillies should be eager to spend after another early elimination, but again, is paying on pitching in their best interest? The Chicago Cubs could certainly use the pitching, but they've never even handed out a $200 million contract. Would they give $300+ million to Skubal? The Toronto Blue Jays have the money and the need for pitching help, but they also just paid Dylan Cease handsomely last winter and finished last in runs scored this past season. A return to the Detroit Tigers would be awesome, but that feels unrealistic.
There're other teams like the San Francisco Giants and the Los Angeles Angels who might show interest, but again, there isn't really a perfect fit. If the Mets and Dodgers won't meet an outlandish asking price, which team will?
The Mets have a clear need for a high-end starting pitcher
The Mets are building a strong rotation, with youngsters like Nolan McLean, Christian Scott and Zac Thornton in the fold, but the team lacks a true ace. They hoped Freddy Peralta would fill that void when they acquired him from the Brewers in the 2025 offseason, but that experiment flopped spectacularly.
It's hard to see Skubal flopping, though, at least in 2027. He remains one of, if not the best pitcher in the sport, and even after an early-season injury scare, Skubal ended his season with a 2.72 ERA in 26 starts. He's as dynamic as they come, and would instantly make the Mets true postseason contenders.
If they don't sign Skubal, who else could they realistically get? The next-best options, such as Michael King, Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes, aren't exactly aces. They could potentially swing a trade, but doing so is easier said than done. It feels like Skubal or bust when it comes to getting a bona fide ace.
Would David Stearns be willing to abandon his starting pitching philosophy to sign Tarik Skubal?
We know that the Mets have the need, the money and the location necessary to lure Skubal to the team, but would the individual responsible for making such a move, David Stearns, be willing to do so? Stearns has famously been averse to handing massive deals to starting pitchers, passing on guys like Corbin Burnes, Max Fried and Dylan Cease, to name a few, and instead relying on shorter-term gambles.
Most of these have not paid off, which is partially why the Mets have missed the playoffs in back-to-back years, but will there be a mindset shift? Will Stearns suddenly go from a guy unwilling to offer more than three years to a pitcher over the age of 30 to willing to meet Skubal's demands?
That's an answer we're soon going to learn the answer to, and it could be the difference in Skubal joining the Mets or signing elsewhere. If Stearns is all in, the stars feel like they're aligning for something special to happen.

item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies absolutely need to bolster their roster this offseason after yet another early playoff exit, but they actually shouldn't be pursuing the biggest fish on the free-agent market.
Tarik Skubal is going to be the top player available this winter, and he will surely have a wide range of suitors. But the Phillies should not be one of them.
Why? Because Philadelphia already boasts one of the best starting rotations in baseball.
The trio of Cristopher Sanchez, Jesus Luzardo and Zack Wheeler is fantastic, and Andrew Painter showed tremendous signs during the second half of the season.
Yes, Aaron Nola is infinitely replaceable, but he did have a strong second half overall, even if his last couple of starts were less than desirable.
Skubal is likely to command $400 million. He's one of the best pitchers in baseball, he's a left-hander and his agent is Scott Boras.
The Phillies have already been monitoring their payroll closely as it is. Their roster is littered with lucrative long-term deals, some of which are not exactly good ones. Do they really want to spend nearly half a billion dollars in an area that doesn't have a need?
Philadelphia needs bats and it needs relievers; period. The Phillies had one of the worst offenses in the league this year, and their bullpen was a disaster down the stretch — and really, for most of the campaign.
That is where Philadelphia should be spending its money.
Sure, the idea of Skubal is tempting. He is a dominant force who won back-to-back Cy Young awards in 2024 and 2025 and just posted a 2.72 ERA and 0.964 WHIP in 2026.
But he's also turning 30 years old next month and has had multiple elbow surgeries. Handing him big-time money over an extended period of time is going to be a significant risk, and it's one that the Phillies really can't take.
Philadelphia's holes are obvious. It must address its outfield, which didn't field a single reliable hitter this season. It needs to find another bat either at second base or third base, depending on where the Phillies want to put Bryson Stott. And they also need to bring in a serviceable catcher alongside J.T. Realmuto.
And of course, it must build a better bridge to Jhoan Duran in the ninth inning.
Skubal does not fill any of those needs. At that cost, it's simply not worth it.

item.title: [Jays Journal] Randy Arozarena’s East Coast preference could put the Blue Jays in the free-agent race
item.dc:creator: Matthew Sookram
item.description: Randy Arozarena’s reported preference to return to the East Coast should immediately grab the attention of the Toronto Blue Jays. The free-agent outfielder makes his home in Tampa, trains in Florida and, according to reports, would prefer to join an eastern team that holds spring training in that state. item.content:encoded:
Randy Arozarena’s reported preference to return to the East Coast should immediately grab the attention of the Toronto Blue Jays. The free-agent outfielder makes his home in Tampa, trains in Florida and, according to reports, would prefer to join an eastern team that holds spring training in that state. Toronto can offer each of those things through its Florida base in Dunedin.
More importantly, the Blue Jays can offer Arozarena an obvious role for 2027 and beyond. Their outfield picture has a lot of uncertainty heading into next year, and the lineup needs precisely what he provides: a right-handed hitter with consistent power, strong on-base skills and enough speed to create pressure once he reaches base.
Randy Arozarena fills several Blue Jays needs at once
Arozarena is coming off the most productive season of his career. He hit .281/.381/.484 with 26 home runs, 79 RBI and 113 runs across 154 games for Seattle, good for an .865 OPS and a 151 wRC+. His 5.5 FanGraphs WAR placed him among the game’s most valuable position players, while his 10.1 per cent walk rate proved he wasn't just swinging for the fences every time up.
The Blue Jays’ current outfield options lean heavily to the left side, with Nathan Lukes, Addison Barger, and Brett Bateman the likely every day guys all hit from the left side. Prospects such as Sean Keys (though limited in the outfield) and Yohendrick Piñango also bat left-handed. Anthony Santander is a switch-hitter but has struggled to stay healthy, while Davis Schneider’s roster status is uncertain at the moment pending the non-tender deadline / arbitration process.
Arozarena would give manager John Schneider a proven right-handed threat that could slot immediately into left-field on an every day basis. And he'd need that bat in there considering how consistent he's been as a slugger over his MLB career. Arozarena has hit at-least 20 home runs in every full season since 2021.
Then there is the speed. Arozarena stole 26 bases in 2026 and has reached the 20-steal mark in six consecutive seasons. Pairing him near the top of the order with Bateman would give the Blue Jays a mix of contact, on-base ability and baserunning they largely lacked outside of Andrés Giménez and Bateman later in the season. Arozarena as a number two hitter behind Bateman could be an immediate recipe for success.
While may no longer be a standout defender in left field, his offence and baserunning would address enough weaknesses to make that trade-off manageable. The other complication lies in the fact that Arozarena could cost the Blue Jays more than just the dollar value he signs.
Arozarena will likely get a one-year qualifying offer from Seattle which is expected to be worth $23.15 million. He would likely reject it in search of a multiyear contract which would then cost the Blue Jays a draft pick. At least, that's how the current system works. If Toronto waits until after the new CBA is signed, that entire structure could change.
But they might not want to wait it out too long. Arozarena’s geographic preference helps the Blue Jays, but it hardly makes Toronto the favourite. The New York Yankees should have many of the same reasons to pursue him. They could move Cody Bellinger out of left field and install Arozarena as another right-handed power bat around Aaron Judge.
Boston also looms as a natural bidder, particularly given Arozarena’s history in the AL East and his career success at Fenway Park. Any market that includes multiple wealthy division rivals could push the contract beyond Toronto’s comfort zone, especially for a player who turns 32 in February.
While Arozarena is not a flawless target and his age creates some risk on a long-term deal, the top of the free agent class is not loaded with stars this winter. The Blue Jays need right-handed power in the outfield and Arozarena has proven he can provide that over his career. The fit makes a ton of sense on paper - whether it comes to fruition or not remains to be seen.

item.title: [Chicago Tribune] Milwaukee Brewers’ NLCS sweep means 2 of MLB’s lower spenders will meet in World Series for 1st time since ’91
item.dc:creator: Ronald Blum
item.description: NEW YORK — When the Milwaukee Brewers defeated the mighty, monied Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday night, they set up the first World Series between two of baseball’s smaller spenders in 35 years — just as team owners are arguing that clubs such as the Brewers need a salary cap to compete consistently. The Brewers will face the Cleveland Guardians or Tampa Bay Rays in a best-of-seven Series for the title beginning Friday, ensuring two clubs in the bottom half of big-league payrolls will play in t
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — When the Milwaukee Brewers defeated the mighty, monied Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday night, they set up the first World Series between two of baseball’s smaller spenders in 35 years — just as team owners are arguing that clubs such as the Brewers need a salary cap to compete consistently.
The Brewers will face the Cleveland Guardians or Tampa Bay Rays in a best-of-seven Series for the title beginning Friday, ensuring two clubs in the bottom half of big-league payrolls will play in the World Series for the first time since 1991. The Dodgers, New York Mets and New York Yankees will watch from home with payrolls this season that each cost more than the Brewers, Guardians and Rays rosters combined.
The low-budget World Series showdown will start six weeks before a likely management lockout, a work stoppage that threatens the 2027 season as owners and players battle over the sport’s lack of a salary cap.
Speaking at the All-Star Game in July, MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred made his case for a cap while saying exceptions did not reflect parity.
“Our view of the world is that over a very long period of time there’s a very strong relationship between who gets into the playoffs and who proceeds, notwithstanding the exceptions we’ve got,” he said.
The Brewers, who won the NL pennant with a four-game sweep of the Dodgers, had MLB’s 19th-highest payroll as of Aug. 31, while the Rays were 25th and Guardians 30th. The last time both pennant winners were among the bottom 50% in player spending was when the Minnesota Twins (15th among 26 teams) beat the Atlanta Braves (19th) for the 1991 championship.
In terms of market size, Milwaukee ranks as MLB’s 30th and smallest Designated Market Area, defined by Nielsen as non-overlapping geographic regions that group counties based on television viewing areas. Cleveland is 22nd and Tampa, Fla., 15th.
If the Guardians win the AL pennant, this would mark the first World Series involving two teams in the bottom half of MLB cities by DMA since the St. Louis Cardinals (24th) beat the Detroit Tigers (18th) in 2006. No small-market team has won the World Series since the Kansas City Royals in 2015.
Three years after the Twins won that 1991 title, players went on strike as owners pushed for a salary cap, leading to the cancellation of the World Series. No such cap was added, and owners hadn’t proposed one again until this summer.
Since the 1991 Twins, the only World Series winners with bottom-half payrolls have been the 2002 Anaheim Angels, 2003 Florida Marlins and 2017 Houston Astros.
“It’s how the game is played in the moment dictates winning outcomes,” agent Scott Boras said Friday. “There’s no question that the probabilities of winning, success, are increased with greater talent, but we all know that talent has many variables as to how it performs at times.”
MLB owners have proposed a salary cap with a floor, a system players say they will never accept. A lockout is likely to start Dec. 2.
Opening-day payrolls were topped by the Mets ($358.4 million), Dodgers ($323.3 million) and Yankees ($302.8 million). The Brewers were at $125.9 million, the Rays $90.5 million and the Guardians $75.5 million.
“Don’t believe what you hear from the owner who’s complaining: ‘I don’t have the resources to compete,’” players association head Bruce Meyer said at the All-Star Game. “They all have the resources to compete. Our proposals include provisions that would give them more resources and reward the teams that actually do compete.”
Manfred maintains spending big increases the odds of success.
“It defies human experience to ask a fan to think that the bottom end of that gap has the same opportunity to win as the top,” he said. “There is no question that everybody in any sport is not going to win once every 30 or 32 years depending on how many teams you have, but the data in our sport is stark: Your opportunity to make the playoffs if you are a larger-market team is dramatically higher and your opportunity to proceed to the subsequent rounds, that advantage grows with each round.”

item.title: [Jays Journal] 3 players the Blue Jays could target if they entertained a Brandon Valenzuela trade
item.dc:creator: Matthew Sookram
item.description: Brandon Valenzuela began the 2026 season as catching depth, but when the season was over he had seemingly solidified himself as the backup catcher for the foreseeable future for the Toronto Blue Jays. What looked like a temporary promotion after Alejandro Kirk fractured his left thumb became a season-long audition in which Valenzuela established himself as an elite defender. He even earned recognition as an American League Gold Glove finalist. That depth is valuable, but it also brings up a legi
item.content:encoded:
Brandon Valenzuela began the 2026 season as catching depth, but when the season was over he had seemingly solidified himself as the backup catcher for the foreseeable future for the Toronto Blue Jays. What looked like a temporary promotion after Alejandro Kirk fractured his left thumb became a season-long audition in which Valenzuela established himself as an elite defender. He even earned recognition as an American League Gold Glove finalist.
That depth is valuable, but it also brings up a legitimate offseason question. With Kirk entrenched as the starter, would the Blue Jays be better served keeping Valenzuela as a high-end backup or using his rising value to address a more pressing need elsewhere on the roster?
Why Valenzuela has real trade value
Valenzuela’s market starts with his defense. In 91 games as a rookie, he ranked among the top five major-league catchers in Statcast Fielding Run Value and FanGraphs’ defensive rating. His framing and blocking gave Toronto’s pitchers a steady target, while his arm helped him throw out 19 of 63 attempted base stealers.
He also held his own at the plate for the first half of the season when he produced a .241/.322/.407 line and a 106 wRC+. Valenzuela’s age and years of club control would certainly be intriguing for prospective teams. Getting a 26-year-old catcher who has already shown he can handle a major-league staff is the type of profile that could be the centre of a decent trade package.
However, there will be detractors around the league. While Valenzuela finished with nine home runs, a double-digit walk rate and a .688 OPS across 271 plate appearances, his second half numbers were not good. He produced a .182/.276/.299 with a 65 wRC+ after the All-Star break. His walk rate held steady, but the strikeouts started to tick up and and he hit just two home runs.
To be fair, rookie catchers often wear down under the physical and mental demands of the position, and teams will likely value his defence first. But it does, limit the return Toronto can reasonably expect. Valenzuela alone is unlikely to fetch an established middle-of-the-order bat or a frontline starter. A more realistic outcome would be a need-for-need deal involving a player with similar control and upside.
What could the Blue Jays get on the trade market for Brandon Valenzuela?
There are several teams that are likely looking for a catcher this offseason and the free agent market is somewhat thin. Three teams that could meet a need-for-need trade are the New York Yankees, Chicago Cubs and Cincinnati Reds.
Yankees - Luis Garcia Jr.
The most ambitious idea would be a deal with the Yankees centred on Luis García Jr. García hit 30 home runs with an .830 OPS in 2026, although his production slipped to a .264/.302/.434 slash line after New York acquired him at the deadline but they are already rumored to be shopping around Garcia this offseason.
His left-handed power would interest Toronto, and returning Garcia back to second base while filling in for Guerrero Jr. at first could address the need to get more pop from the right side of the infield.
The Yankees would almost certainly demand more than Valenzuela in return. But they are also desperate to upgrade on Austin Wells behind the dish and they will need to potentially replace other players such as Trent Grisham, Jazz Chisholm, David Bednar, and Paul Goldschmidt just to name a few.
Cubs - Kevin Alcántara
Chicago is potentially losing Carson Kelly behind the plate, putting the Cubs in need of a replacement. Kevin Alcántara is a 24-year-old right-handed outfielder that will be fighting for playing time with the South Siders. Alcántara hit 20 home runs with an .852 OPS at Triple-A in 2026.
The power and handedness should intrigue Toronto who currently only has two MLB outfielders who bat from the right side and that's Anthony Santander (a switch-hitter and outfielder is a loose term with him) and Davis Schenider (who could be a non-tender candidate).
It could be risky to move a proven MLB backup catcher (at worst) in Valenzuela for Alcántara who has yet to stick around in the big leagues after 37 games over three stints dating back to 2024. But the Blue Jays need some flexibility in their outfield corps and after the Blue Jays had so much success with their last trade with the Cubs they might be wise to go to the well again.
Reds - JJ Bleday
JJ Bleday represents another version of the same need-for-need framework. The Cincinnati outfielder hit .217/.324/.416 with 24 home runs and 72 walks in 2026. Again, the pop is the selling point here and he's under team control through 2028.
His significant second-half drop and stronger production against right-handed pitching make him more of a platoon-oriented corner bat and, as stated, the Blue Jays already have a few of those in Nathan Lukes, Addison Barger, Sean Keys and Yohendrick Piñango. Still, if Cincinnati decides it needs a defensive upgrade behind the plate, Valenzuela could form the foundation of a conversation.
Keeping Valenzuela may still be the better move
The strongest argument against a trade is Kirk’s 2026 injury. Toronto learned how quickly catching depth can derail a season. Valenzuela helped stabilize a key piece of the Blue Jays roster and held his own.
There is also room for both catchers. Kirk is the clear starter, but carrying Valenzuela would allow Toronto to protect him from overuse and they could use either catcher at designated hitter on occasion
Valenzuela has enough value that the Blue Jays should not make him untouchable, and if another club is willing to exchange a controllable everyday outfielder, or a credible second-base option, Toronto would be justified in using its catching depth to improve a thinner area of the roster.
But dealing him simply because Kirk is ahead of him would be a mistake. Valenzuela’s defence, affordability and ability to step into a larger role give the Blue Jays more certainty than most teams possess behind their starting catcher. Unless the return clearly improves the 2027 roster, keeping one of baseball’s better defensive catching tandems is the safer—and probably smarter—choice.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Phillies Boss Pinpoints ‘Really, Really Good’ Infield Replacement After Trea Turner Decision
item.dc:creator: Peter Chawaga; Contributor
item.description: The Philadelphia Phillies head into yet another offseason with questions to answer about their roster construction after an early postseason exit. Earlier this week, during his end of season press conference, president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski made it clear that the team needs to improve defensively, and one of its biggest decisions could involve a veteran who remains central to the franchise. "From a defensive perspective, we are very clear," Dombrowski said of Trea Turner, accord
item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies head into yet another offseason with questions to answer about their roster construction after an early postseason exit.
Earlier this week, during his end of season press conference, president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski made it clear that the team needs to improve defensively, and one of its biggest decisions could involve a veteran who remains central to the franchise.
"From a defensive perspective, we are very clear," Dombrowski said of Trea Turner, according to the New York Post's Matt Ehalt. "He knows he has to be better at shortstop. And I told him that it's really mandatory that he's like that."
Though Dombrowski made it clear that Turner no longer has a lock on the shortstop position, the Phillies seem reliant on the long-term contracts already on the books, including his. But during the same press conference, the front office boss singled out one new player who could join the roster next season.
Philadelphia Phillies Boss Highlights Trea Turner Replacement After Harsh Warning
If Turner cannot return to his previous defensive form, Dombrowski made it clear that he will consider other options. Initially, it seems most likely that the team would shift Turner to second base or to the outfield and move Bryson Stott to shortstop.
But the Phillies president also pinpointed an exciting young infielder as an example of a new player who could join the mix next season.
"I'm not going to put it on his back, but we think a guy like Aidan Miller is a really, really good player," Dombrowski said, according to MLB.com's Todd Zolecki. "You see all the young players that have jumped into playing this year and the years that they had. Aidan Miller, when he's healthy, he's as good as any of them."
Turner is entering the fourth season of his 11-year, $300 million contract, and the Phillies have not ruled out keeping him at shortstop. But Dombrowski singled out Miller as an intriguing option to take some pressure off of the team's veteran core of position players, and it seems that if and when he does receive a promotion, he could be taking over the shortstop role.
Philadelphia Phillies' Trea Turner Replacement Could Already Be In The Organization
Miller's potential makes him an interesting name to watch as the Phillies consider their infield options, although his arrival should not be viewed as a certainty for Opening Day.
The prospect entered 2026 as Philadelphia's top-ranked position prospect but lost much of the season to a back injury that required surgery in June. He returned to action in September, appearing in four regular-season games across the Florida Complex League and Double-A Reading before helping Reading during its Eastern League championship run.
For now, Turner has an opportunity to retain his position by improving defensively. But with Dombrowski publicly identifying Miller as a potential contributor, the Phillies have another avenue to explore if their veteran shortstop cannot deliver the necessary improvement.
This article was originally published on Forbes.com

item.title: [inquirer.com] Sorry, Phillies fans, Dave Dombrowski is not going anywhere | Marcus Hayes
item.dc:creator: Marcus Hayes
item.description: Skip to content Sorry, Phillies fans, Dave Dombrowski is not going anywhere for a long, long time. Is that a bad thing? Dealin' Dave, President for Life, denied offering a job to Alex Cora, said Trea Turner must audition at shortstop, and said the farm system is A-OK. Seriously: I hope John Middleton never fires him. If you’re a Dave Dombrowski hater, no matter where you were or what you were doing, your blood ran cold Thursday morning. That was when the Phillies president of baseball operations
item.content:encoded:
Skip to content
Sorry, Phillies fans, Dave Dombrowski is not going anywhere for a long, long time. Is that a bad thing?
Dealin' Dave, President for Life, denied offering a job to Alex Cora, said Trea Turner must audition at shortstop, and said the farm system is A-OK. Seriously: I hope John Middleton never fires him.
If you’re a Dave Dombrowski hater, no matter where you were or what you were doing, your blood ran cold Thursday morning. That was when the Phillies president of baseball operations, in his post-season news conference, blithely remarked:
“I plan on being here for a while. I enjoy it. I’m healthy. I have quality people around me.”
In a town whose football team has lost three straight and whose coach blew the last game in the last 8 seconds; whose basketball team hasn’t gotten past the second round of the playoffs in 25 years; and whose hockey team is winless in its first nine games, Dombrowski is, by far, the most despised sports figure.
And he’s here for the long haul.
Marcus Hayes alerts
During his 61-minute, end-of-season news conference, Dombrowski addressed important issues: Trea Turner’s pending and overdue removal from the shortstop position; his unwillingness to trade from among the starting pitching but his willingness to trade star hitters if those hitters were willing; announcements that Don Mattingly will return as manager and turnover on the coaching staff; and his faith in a minor-league system that he believes is incorrectly rated among the worst in baseball.
But his own future, both long- and short-term, was the most significant issue of the day.
Is that a bad thing? Most Phillies fans, in this moment, would answer, resoundingly, “Yes.”
The backstory
Dombrowski took the Phillies to the World Series in 2022, his second season, but playoff collapses in the following four seasons authored mainly by Dombrowski’s porous bullpens and choking hitters put a target on his back that even José Alvarado could hit. This year, as the Phillies faded from the top wild-card slot to the final wild-card slot to a three-game wild-card exit in Atlanta, Dombrowski’s star sank lower than ever in every corner of Philadelphia ... except one. It’s the only corner that matters.
It’s the office of John Middleton, the Phillies’ managing partner.
Middleton adores Dombrowski. Last month, following up a report by The Athletic that Dombrowski will soon receive an extension beyond his current deal’s expiration in 2027, I was told by a Phillies source, “Middleton will never fire Dombrowski.”
» READ MORE: Don Mattingly ‘carried the stick.’ That helped make him the best choice as Phillies manager.
A few days later, USA Today reported that the Phillies will offer Dombrowski a lifetime contract, presumably to fill whatever role he desires. Right now, at the age of 70, he still desires to decide who’s on the roster and who’s managing them.
Has he earned it? Not in Philadelphia, no. But elsewhere, Dombrowski won two World Series and went to two more. Middleton adores him; essentially, in Middleton’s eyes, Dombrowski can do no wrong.
In my eyes, Dombrowski’s been about average. He inherited an organization that included Bryce Harper, Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sánchez, Aaron Nola, J.T. Realmuto, Alec Bohm, and Bryson Stott.
He’s extended some of those deals, signed Kyle Schwarber (twice), enhanced the roster with trades for Jesús Luzardo and Jhoan Duran, and hit on deadline deals for Harrison Bader in 2025 and Luis Arraez in 2026 (both were hurt in the playoffs, though).
He also has consistently failed to replace the right-handed power of Rhys Hoskins, has shown abominable judgment in bullpen construction, and, in seeking optimal offensive output, has inexcusably and illogically devalued defense, especially for a team so heavily invested in big-money starting pitching: He has four $100 million starters.
Further, the contracts of outfielder Nick Castellanos, a defensive liability, Turner, a defensive liability, and starter Taijuan Walker, the ultimate defensive liability, proved utterly indefensible.
Still, as Middleton loves to point out, any president who takes a team to the playoffs five years in a row must be doing something right.
» READ MORE: To Dave Dombrowski, the Phillies’ problems begin an arm’s length away
Counterpoint: In Dombrowski’s case, so far, most of what he’s done right is that he hasn’t messed with what former GM Matt Klentak left him.
Also: If the Phillies are such a quality team with such a bright future, why did Alex Cora, the manager who won Dombrowski the 2018 World Series in Boston, turn down the manager’s job twice in six months? Does he want to win Puerto Rico the Father of the Year this badly?
Furthermore, if Dombrowski was such a hotshot executive, why did the Sox fire him less than 11 months after winning it all?
None of those questions matter. What matters is, John hearts Dave.
Madness ensues
I, for one, am happy that Dombrowski is sticking around. That’s mainly because I, for one, don’t care if the Phillies win every game, lose every game, or have every game rained out, as long as they’re interesting while doing it.
Also, I enjoy talking to Dombrowski. He’s smart, intriguing, and his hair has its own aura, as the kids say.
Besides, how can I endorse firing a guy who I’m giving a grade like “C?” You know, average. You fire guys who get D’s and F’s.
That “C” grade means Dombrowski probably does a better job at roster building than, say, I, who am a connoisseur of shortstops (and point guards); a far better job than, say Mike Sielski, whose expertise is limited to hockey centermen; but probably not as good a job as David Murphy, who obsesses on wRC+ and FIP (and who, incongruently, is a quarterback aficionado, too).
» READ MORE: Phillies will keep Trea Turner at shortstop for now: ‘He knows he has to be better’
Also, Dombrowski says crazy stuff.
He fired Rob Thomson and, after being turned down by Cora, the fired former Red Sox manager, he replaced Thomson with Mattingly, the bench coach, as interim manager.
Dombrowski said Thursday that, while he’d followed a baseball mandate and interviewed other candidates, he had never offered the job to anyone but Mattingly. He said this with a straight face ... after both USA Today and the Phillies’ own website reported that, early last week, Cora had turned him down again.
Dombrowski on Thursday also said he actually signed Mattingly to a deal last Saturday, but, with the Eagles playing Sunday (24 hours later) and with Mattingly lacking solid internet service at his vacation lodgings, they delayed leaking the news until Wednesday ... so as to have better Wi-Fi on Thursday for Mattingly’s Zoom news conference.
I am not making any of that up.
Old MacDonald’s farm
Dombrowski also tried to convince listeners that their farm system is better than the experts rank it, which is generally between fifth-to-last and second-to-last. He asserted that major league rookies Andrew Painter, Justin Crawford, and Alex McFarlane should count toward their farm depth, and that they should be credited for using prospects to acquire Luzardo and Duran.
Dombrowski ignored the fact that Painter and Crawford did not factor into the current rankings at all, and he ignored the fact that teams ranked higher than his also traded prospects to improve. For instance, the Dodgers traded three prospects at the deadline to acquire Tarik Skubal from the Tigers, two of them ranked in the top 100 by MLB.com, and still had an elite system at the season’s end. The Brewers also traded prospects for bullpen help at the deadline, and their farm system remains as good or better than the Dodgers’ — whom they just swept out of the NLCS.
Coup de grace
The nuttiest thing Dombrowski said in his hourlong State of the Union regarded Turner. By most metrics, Turner was, by far, the worst defensive shortstop in all of baseball. Dombrowski’s solution:
He forced Turner to leave his home in Florida and travel to Philadelphia for a two-hour meeting with Dombrowski, which is like a kid on summer break getting called back to school to go to the principal’s office. What did they talk about for two hours? Some of it concerned Turner’s career-worst offensive performance, which is weird, since that’s kind of the job of the manager and the hitting coach. Some of it concerned Turner’s defense.
Dombrowski warned Turner that Turner would have to audition in spring training if he hopes to retain the shortstop job. Otherwise, he will be moved, most likely to left field, though Turner would prefer staying on the infield, most likely at second base.
» READ MORE: The most imaginative changes the Phillies can make begin with moving Trea Turner off shortstop
What?
WHAT?
So, the plan to return the 33-year-old’s defensive skills from putridity back to their heights, which were mediocrity, is to have him walk on eggshells for 20 spring training games? In which he will play, what, a total of 90 innings — 90 innings that Turner could spend acclimating himself to second base, where he’s started just 79 games, or left field where he’s played zero games?
Assume Turner exits spring training as the shortstop, then he commits four errors in April — again. Do you banish him to the grass or push him to the right side of the infield in the middle of the season? What chance does he have to succeed in that sort of atmosphere?
Of all the harebrained schemes the Phillies have hatched in the past 15 years or so, the plan for Turner is the wildest. Really, this stuff just writes itself. Thanks, Dave.
And, Mr. Middleton: To hell with your fans. For my sake, and for the sake of columnists everywhere, please never fire Dave Dombrowski.

item.title: [Sporting News JP] NLCS最優秀選手賞（MVP）歴代受賞者リスト｜MLBポストシーズン - スポーティングニュース
item.dc:creator: 佐藤瑞紀 Mizuki Sato

item.title: [puckettspond.com] This year's World Series shows where the Twins have failed
item.dc:creator: Chris Schad

item.content:encoded:
The Minnesota Twins have spent another October watching the postseason from home and the biggest question is why. The Twins have missed the playoffs in five of the past six seasons and while many are rightfully upset about the team’s payroll slashing, there are also several fundamental mistakes that have prevented them from being successful.
Those mistakes will be front and center during this year’s World Series. The Milwaukee Brewers punched their ticket to the Fall Classic after completing a sweep over the Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday night and they will face either the Tampa Bay Rays or Cleveland Guardians in what will be a showdown between small-market teams.
While this year’s matchup could create a loophole for the Pohlad family to avoid dropping a large amount of money to improve the team, it also reflects poorly on their decisions that have kept them from competing over the past few years.
The Brewers, Rays and Guardians are showing the Twins how to build a winner
As you may have guessed, the Brewers, Guardians and Rays are not among MLB’s biggest spenders. According to Cot’s Baseball Contracts, the Brewers’ year-end salary ranked 23rd at $99.3 million and defeated the Dodgers’ No. 1 roster at $366.0 million. The American League finalists were also budget-conscious as the Rays ranked 20th with a year-end payroll of $103.1 million and the Guardians ranked 25th at $91.0 million.
All three of the remaining teams had a lower year-end payroll than the Twins, who ranked 17th with a figure of $123.9 million and while many, including owner and chairman Tom Pohlad, believe that adding to that number could lead to a championship, the other three teams show what they have done wrong.
The first is maximizing the value of players on the roster. The Rays, Guardians and Brewers have traded players before they get to free agency to add to their organization and it’s paid off in a big way. The Brewers most notably did this in a February 2024 trade featuring Corbin Burnes that brought back left-hander DL Hall and infielder Joey Ortiz.
The Rays also have done this with their trade of Triple-A right-hander Tobias Myers, who was traded to Cleveland as he was eligible for the Rule 5 Draft in 2021, and brought back star third baseman Junior Caminero in return. While the Guardians whiffed on Myers, they made other shrewd deals that netted them Craig Yoho, Patrick Bailey, Foster Griffin and Kyle Manzardo.
These trades are a double-edged sword as they usually involve popular players. But it brings back pieces that ensure a larger championship window. That leaves player development as the final phase of the three contenders and each team has a homegrown star to lean on such as Jose Ramirez, Jacob Misiorowski or Caminero.
The Twins’ biggest problems go beyond their payroll
Turning the attention back to the Twins, it’s easy to see where they have come up short. This year’s trade deadline was one opportunity to shift the narrative. But instead of trading players that could bring back a big return such as Ryan Jeffers and Joe Ryan, the Twins went the opposite direction, adding A.J. Minter, Jeff Hoffman and Dean Kremer.
Even when they tried to trade Trevor Larnach to the Houston Astros before owner Jim Crane vetoed it, they were seeking 29-year-old Bryan Abreu, a pitcher who posted his highest ERA (3.73) and lowest WAR (1.0) since his rookie season in 2021.
The other key issue is the Twins’ player development. While top prospects such as Royce Lewis and Matt Wallner thrive initially when reaching the major leagues, those players have hit a wall when pitchers adjust to them. The problem can be traced back to Miguel Sano’s downfall in the early 2020s and can still be seen in a group of post-hype hitters that haven’t lived up to their prospect status.
This leaves the Twins in a tricky spot this offseason. After failing to trade Jeffers at the deadline, there’s a good chance he’ll leave in free agency. Ryan has a year of team control remaining, but trading him now could get a pair of MLB-ready players in return. Several top prospects including Walker Jenkins, Emmanuel Rodriguez and Kaelen Culpepper made their debuts this season, but the key will be to make sure they don’t regress entering their first full season in the bigs.
Of course, fans may cheer for a salary floor to hold the Pohlads accountable for what happens to the Twins next. But the Rays, Guardians and Brewers show that paying top dollar may not be necessary to build a contender and Minnesota would be wise to follow their blueprint.

item.content:encoded:
After two seasons that ended in the same Wild Card elimination by the same team in the same stadium, upgrading the offense should be the Boston Red Sox's No. 1 priority. There's so much depth in their lineup that there isn't an exceedingly obvious place to add, but it's long been established that their outfield group needs to be shrunk.
Following a career-worst season during which he was one of the worst qualified hitters in the league, trading Jarren Duran seems like an easy answer. Finding a suitor for him after a severe offensive regression and multiple instances of off-the-field drama won't be easy, however.
But MLB insider Jon Heyman reports there's still interest in Duran from one team — the one we all expect. Heyman said in his Bleacher Report live stream that the San Diego Padres are still interested in the outfielder.
The Friars have long expressed their desire to trade for Duran. They've publicly been the team most interested in dealing for him, though there could be others behind the scenes. San Diego once offered Boston Dylan Cease, top catching prospect Ethan Salas and one other prospect for Duran, which the Red Sox "quickly rejected," according to Sean McAdam of MassLive.
MLB insider Jon Heyman says Padres are still interested in Jarren Duran trade with Red Sox
Cease would've just been a rental, but the Red Sox should've taken that deal. They could've extended Cease, but Duran's value was never going to increase — time is ticking down on his contract and he had never shown that he could maintain the level of offensive production he had in 2024, when he earned the All-Star Game MVP and came in eighth in American League MVP voting.
The Padres are likely to lose outfielders Miguel Andujar, Austin Hays and Ramón Laureano to the free agent market, meaning they could use another body in their pastures. Duran's .207/.266/.361 slash line and 165 strikeouts over 151 games are hardly encouraging, but he's a prime change-of-scenery candidate and he could rebound elsewhere.
Boston must prioritize trading Duran (and Masataka Yoshida) not only to give it lineup flexibility, but to open its designated hitter spot for a power bat rather than maintaining the rotating DH structure that it's gone with in recent years. The Red Sox need their top hitters in the lineup every day, and signing or trading for someone who could swap between DH and left field with Roman Anthony is seemingly the easiest way to add power to the lineup.
Trading Duran is also the optimal outcome this offseason because he's regressed so severely that he could be a non-tender risk. At least trading him to the Padres would net the Red Sox a return, however small.
The Red Sox need to clear their outfield logjam if they're serious about improving their offense. Trading Duran should be the first step to their upswing.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Rays Need Junior Caminero to Wake Up Before It's Too Late
item.dc:creator: Christian Rauh
item.description: The Tampa Bay Rays are now facing a difficult situation in the American League Championship Series after falling 3-2 to the Cleveland Guardians in Game 3 on Thursday. Especially Junior Caminero. The Rays' star slugger had arguably his worst performance of the season against Cleveland, going 0-for-4 with four strikeou
item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays are now facing a difficult situation in the American League Championship Series after falling 3-2 to the Cleveland Guardians in Game 3 on Thursday.
And while there are plenty of things to criticize about the performance, I think the biggest concern continues to be the lack of offensive production from Tampa Bay's biggest stars.
Especially Junior Caminero.
The Rays' star slugger had arguably his worst performance of the season against Cleveland, going 0-for-4 with four strikeouts.
And it wasn't necessarily because Gavin Williams was throwing pitches that were impossible to hit. Caminero consistently took hittable pitches early in counts before chasing balls well outside the strike zone.
That's something we haven't seen much of throughout the regular season. A year where he has surely earned votes for American League MVP.
And I think it's fair to wonder whether Caminero is trying to do too much at the plate.
The 45-home-run slugger still hasn't hit a home run this postseason, and his batting average sits at .238 with a .666 OPS.
Those numbers certainly aren't what Tampa Bay needs from one of its biggest offensive weapons.
But Caminero isn't the only player struggling.
Yandy Díaz is hitting .240 with a .589 OPS, while Jonathan Aranda has managed just a .182 batting average and .568 OPS.
Victor Mesa Jr. is hitting .143, and Liam Hicks isn't doing much better at .167.
These are supposed to be the players carrying Tampa Bay's offense.
Instead, the Rays have relied on contributions from the bottom of their lineup.
Chandler Simpson delivered Tampa Bay's only two runs Thursday with an impressive two-RBI triple against Williams.
Richie Palacios has also provided some important hits, while Jonny DeLuca has been one of Tampa Bay's more productive hitters throughout the series.
But that can't continue being the expectation.
Tampa Bay won 98 games during the regular season because it had a lineup capable of consistently putting the baseball in play and creating scoring opportunities.
However, the Rays have yet to score more than four runs in a postseason game.
And Thursday might've been the most frustrating example.
Tampa Bay managed just three hits and struck out 13 times, including seven strikeouts from the top of the batting order.
The Rays also went down in order in seven of their nine offensive innings.
That's not going to get the job done in October.
Especially against a Cleveland team that has consistently taken advantage of its opportunities.
Now, I'm not suggesting Tampa Bay's season is over.
The Rays are only trailing 2-1 in a seven-game series, and there's still plenty of baseball left to play.
But if Tampa Bay wants to reach the World Series, its biggest offensive stars need to start playing like it.
And that starts with Junior Caminero.

item.content:encoded:
New York radio host Tommy Lugauer has made a strong case for the New York Yankees to pursue San Diego Padres star Fernando Tatis Jr. in a blockbuster trade. Lugauer argued that the outfielder could address several of the team's roster concerns.
The Yankees' 2026 postseason campaign ended with a 3-0 sweep by the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League Division Series, extending their World Series drought to 17 seasons. New York entered the playoffs as the No. 4 seed after finishing the regular season with a 93-68 record, second in the AL East behind Tampa Bay.
Following the disappointing postseason exit, Lugauer discussed the Yankees' offseason priorities during a segment on WFAN Sports Radio. He argued that acquiring the $340 million star should be at the top of the team's list, praising the 27-year-old's offensive production, defensive ability, and potential fit in New York.
"The Yankees' top priority in the offseason should be doing everything in their power to acquire Fernando Tatis Jr. Tatis would solve a million issues for the Yankees. Leadoff hitter clutch, an electric player defensively, offensively. I think Fernando Tatis Junior would be a rock star in New York, a rock star. And he should be their future right fielder for the Yankees," said Lugauer.
He added:
"Judge is to either DH or first base, and or maybe a combination of both. Right field's going to be wide open, and who better to man right field for years to come with the Yankees than Tatis?"
Fernando Tatis last played in the 2026 postseason on October 7, when the Padres lost 3-1 to the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 4 of the National League Division Series, ending San Diego's season.
Fernando Tatis Jr. reflects on the Padres' 2026 season
After the San Diego Padres lost to the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 4 of the NLDS and got eliminated from the playoffs, Fernando Tatis Jr. spoke to reporters about what he had learned throughout the season and his determination to keep improving.
The outfielder emphasized his commitment to growing both on and off the field, while continuing to work toward delivering the results San Diego's fans expect.
"It's a lot of learning experience. I was just gonna put it that way, you know, this game will teach you so many stuff on and off the field every single year, so at my disposal. Simple servant, I'm just here to keep learning every single year to keep getting better as a person, as a man. As a father, you know, and we're just gonna keep battling and find a way to give San Diego what they really deserve," said Tatis.
Fernando Tatis finished the 2026 regular season with 181 hits and 96 runs scored across 159 games, recording 626 at-bats.

item.title: [mlb.com] Who should Brewers want to face in the World Series?
item.dc:creator: Zach Sweet

item.content:encoded:
When the Brewers finished off the Dodgers on Thursday night, their World Series opponent was the last thing on anyone’s mind. An MLB official closed the postgame press conference by telling manager Pat Murphy and NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, “We’ll see you in Milwaukee at the World Series.”
Murphy’s reply said everything: “When’s that start?”
Next Friday, Oct. 23, at American Family Field, where Milwaukee holds home-field advantage thanks to its franchise-record 103 wins. The Guardians took a 2-1 ALCS lead over the Rays into Friday night's scheduled Game 4 at Progressive Field. Milwaukee, meanwhile, will have a full week to rest, which leaves plenty of time to watch and wonder.
Here’s a guide to each potential matchup. You decide which one you’d rather see.
If the regular season is a guide ...
It doesn’t tell us much. The Brewers went 2-1 against both teams.
Milwaukee won the first two games against Cleveland on June 16-17 before rookie left-hander Parker Messick struck out nine over six innings in the finale. Cleveland was without José Ramírez, Angel Martínez and Chase DeLauter. All three are back.
When the Brewers hit
Milwaukee’s lineup is built on pressure. The Brewers ranked in the top five in doubles, runs, hits, walks, batting average and on-base percentage.
That approach might get more of a test against Tampa Bay. The Rays issued the fewest walks in the Majors (409) and ranked second in defensive runs saved (87). Drawing walks and finding holes gets tougher against that combination. And their top starters have carried it into October: Drew Rasmussen has a 1.29 ERA through two postseason starts, while Peralta has allowed one earned run in 10 2/3 innings, including six shutout innings in Game 2 of the ALCS.
Cleveland offers a different challenge. Gavin Williams has been a monster, striking out 33 over 16 2/3 innings this postseason. The Guardians have a 2.54 ERA this October, slightly better than Tampa Bay’s 2.72. But Cleveland issued 530 regular-season walks to the Rays’ 409, giving Milwaukee more reason to believe its patient approach can create traffic.
When the other side hits
The regular-season numbers favor facing Cleveland. The Guardians had the lowest OPS (.696) and fewest runs (678) of any postseason team. Tampa Bay offered a more complete attack, with Junior Caminero’s 42 homers anchoring a lineup that tied for fifth in on-base percentage (.326).
October has told a different story. Through Thursday, Cleveland was averaging 4.25 runs per game with a .685 OPS, compared with Tampa Bay’s 3.00 runs and .563 OPS. The Guardians haven’t suddenly become an offensive powerhouse, but they’ve been more productive than the Rays, whose lineup managed just three hits in Game 3 of the ALCS.
The larger sample still points toward Cleveland as the preferable opponent. The way these teams are hitting right now makes that a tougher call.
The bullpens
Neither ninth inning looks inviting. Tampa Bay’s Bryan Baker has saved all four Rays wins this postseason without allowing a hit in four innings. Ian Seymour has been a strong bridge, allowing one earned run in 6 1/3 innings.
Cleveland counters with Cade Smith, who has allowed two hits and one run while striking out 13 in nine innings this October. Hunter Gaddis has added six scoreless innings across seven appearances. Both teams have arms capable of shortening games.
The Brewers have made a habit of coming back this postseason, and their bats have shown they can pick at a bullpen late. Against either opponent, getting a lead before the closer enters would make life easier.
What about the intangibles?
The Guardians’ championship drought dates to 1948. The Rays, like the Brewers, have never won a World Series.
The Rays mirror Milwaukee in many ways. Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold worked in Tampa Bay’s front office alongside current Rays GM Erik Neander. Add Peralta facing his former team, and the storyline writes itself.
Cleveland manager Stephen Vogt played for Milwaukee and interviewed for the job that went to Murphy three years ago. And a Cleveland-Milwaukee World Series comes with a built-in movie reference: Major League, filmed in Milwaukee with Bob Uecker’s Harry Doyle calling Cleveland's improbable run.
The verdict
Give the Guardians a slight edge as Milwaukee’s preferred opponent, though their October bats have made that a tougher sell. The Rays were the more complete team over six months. Cleveland has spent the past two weeks making those six months feel a little less relevant.
The Brewers? They just sent the back-to-back champs home. They’ll let the AL sort this out. Somebody remind Murph what time Friday’s game starts.
